Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. If I had not been recognized today, I would not be raising it. I say that because I would not want it to be understood that I am making a representation on behalf of myself. This is the third occasion in the past three months on which I have raised this question.
I wish to again point out there are one or two rules in the House of Commons which I and most members feel supersede any specific rule that might exist. One is freedom of speech which is referred to extensively by all of the great writers on parliamentary procedure. It is frequently pointed out in Beauchesne that the rule of absolute rigidity has no place in the House of Commons. It is important to remember these paramount rules and call them to mind once in a while.
The House of Commons today is governed by a number of rules with regard to asking questions and the parameters of the question period. One would almost have to be a criminal lawyer with years of professional training in order to conform to the rules which govern asking questions. If Your Honour were to apply to the letter the rules that exist, no member would be able to ask a question. I
Oral Questions
am not reflecting on the Chair, but on the application and the interpretation of the rules.
It is now seven months since the matter was raised. Since the new rules were brought in four years ago, there have been dozens of representations in an attempt to eneble members to ask their questions in a way that does not frustrate them, their constituencies or the country. To date, we have not received a report. I do not know if there have been discussions among the various House leaders.
I am convinced that the rules of this House of Commons are making it very difficult for members to carry out their duties. We are constantly reminded of the fact there are too many supplementaries. There are not too many supple-mentaries. The problem is that we are confined to a 40 minute question period. Consequently, members feel guilty for pursuing a matter because it prohibits their colleagues from asking questions. It is necessary to pursue many questions in detail in order to keep the government on its toes. This is the responsibility of the opposition. We are cut off in the middle of our pursuit because of the 40 minute limitation.
I see no reason why it should take several months to make some minor adjustments to the rules regarding the question period. I am firmly convinced that if the question period were extended, members would find their own level of responsibility. After a few weeks, once the momentum of their questions died down, there would not be this problem with the question period. For almost 100 years there was no time limit on the question period. We must assume that for almost 100 years members of parliament were responsible, but for the past four years members have been denied the justice they deserve under the most important rules of this House. I feel guilty every time I try to ask a question. I know that by doing so, my colleagues may be denied the opportunity because of the 40 minute limit.
As things now stand, we could go on from twelve o'clock until five this afternoon killing time for most of the day with only 15 or 20 members in the House, often not even a quorum, without anyone in the country knowing what is going on. Yet this most important aspect of the work of the House of Commons, holding the government accountable for its actions, is cut off after 40 minutes. I should like to think I am speaking for all members, including members of the government party, when I say we can wait no longer for the results of the long drawn-out process of considering this matter in the committee on procedure. I think the House leaders, with some feeling that members are being gypped, must get their heads together, perhaps accept an interim report from the committee and bring about an immediate change in the rules.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was pointing out yesterday, on the occasion of the preliminary report submitted and published by the Electoral Boundaries Commission it became evident that there was an increase in the total number of Ontario seats by three: unfortunately, the net increase for the southern portion of Ontario was five seats, two being taken away from the northern portion.
To the best of my recollection, every member from northern Ontario made representations to the commission in order to express displeasure not only at the redistribution as effected but also at the loss of two of the 12 seats. I must say that the commissioners were very attentive to the representations made, probably because of the quality of the representations of members from northern Ontario as well as the unity of opinion which they communicated. Indeed, the commissioners suggested that perhaps the commission should return to the drawing board in order to salvage two seats which had been taken away following the application of the principles of the statute as it stood. It took them some time to reconsider the matter, and they did salvage one of the two seats which had been taken away. However, in doing so they produced an abortion of considerable dimensions.
If we look at the redistribution determined under schedule C of the report tabled in the House yesterday, we find that the district of Albany-Nipigon now starts at Hudson Bay and stretches right down to Lake Superior, encompassing roughly 40 per cent of the province of Ontario. And that is one constituency. I am not alleging any bad faith on the part of the commissioners. Indeed, they were very serious in the consideration of the submissions which had been made. Those submissions were basically that northern Ontario is an area in the province which is most apt to be developed in the near future, and that in these circumstances it is essential that it have adequate representation, as was indicated by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding). This point was well made, and it was accepted. However, there are inherent limitations imposed by the statute as it exists today. The commissioners were limited by the 25 per cent provi-

sion, one which they could not vary, and they attempted to abide by our request while finding it almost impossible to do so in accordance with the principles laid down in the act. It is therefore a matter of satisfaction to me that steps should be taken by the government to forestall the effect of redistribution at this time for a period of 18 months.
As I pointed out yesterday, if the present trend toward urbanization continues we shall find ourselves by the year 2000 with a concentration of population within large urban centres whose location has now been established. The power of the House of Commons in a federated state is very strong, it is true, but it is a limited power since the provincial governments share jurisdiction. The provincial governments are located in the urban centres to which I have referred; their realm of influence lies within these centres. The civil servants of the provinces are located in the same centres. As a result of the concentration of population in these areas, the media of information must focus attention on them. Those whose role is the formation of public opinion are located in these areas. All economic decisions made by corporate entities are reached in these urban centres. Decisions of the courts are directed toward the interests of those centres.
If we take into consideration the whole gamut of power as exercised in a free society we find that the government is but one level of that power. Public opinion is another. Presentation of the news exercises part of that power. The economic decision-makers exercise another. If the present trend continues we shall find that all decisions are made in our urban centres. I would remind hon. members of the comment made by a member of one of our major urban centres the other day, that he found it remarkable that we only talked about fish and wheat in this House. I suggest to him that with this increase of power in the urban centres, the day will come when we shall not talk about fish and wheat any more; we shall not even be concerned about fish and wheat, much less about such things as the gold mining assistance legislation or legislation to reduce regional disparity. Such measures were enacted, I suggest, because hon. members directly affected by the necessity for them pressed the government and obliged it to place legislation on the statute books.
If we are heading toward a position where all decisions are made by members from urban centres, we shall no doubt develop in Canada the best of rapid transit systems from Ottawa to Toronto or from Montreal to Saint John. But we shall forget about transportation issues; we shall forget about the equalization of freight rates.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a rather unique situation to find myself in this particular instance very much in accord with the remarks of the previous speaker. I find there is a great deal of difficulty
July 6, 1973

in trying to convey to the urban areas of Canada the complications of rural representation in the House of Commons. I believe there is some misunderstanding here, so let us hope this debate helps to resolve it and get a misunderstanding-it is not a conflict but merely a misunderstanding-into its proper light.
One speaker in this debate said that only the members of the House of Commons are concerned about redistribution-not the people of the constituencies but the members themselves who are trying to serve their own selfish interests. I categorically deny that statement. It is not in line with the feelings in the constituency from which I come.
At a hearing on January 29 in the city of Fredericton, New Brunswick, of an Electoral Boundaries Commission, several organizations in the riding of Carleton in which I live presented views in respect of their disapproval of the boundary map as it was drawn. Those are the representations of the people of my constituency: they do not like the map as it is drawn, and they do not think it gives proper consideration to their interests or will in the long run give them proper representation here.
There were several unique things in the report in respect of New Brunswick that were subject to criticism. For instance, when the commission undertook this redistribution program it found there were four constituencies in New Brunswick approaching the minimal population for proper representation under the act. When the commission was through, it ended up with four constituencies in New Brunswick again with the minimal population required under the act. So there was very little accomplished. This was pointed out to the commission at the hearing in Fredericton on January 29.
I should like to go a little further in discussing that hearing. I made representations on behalf of the people in my constituency. I listened also to the representations made by a professor of the University of New Brunswick on behalf of the Liberal Party in that area. I think the identically parallel position which the two of us presented to the commission should indicate to this House, if the hearing were reviewed, that there is unanimity of thought as to the purposes and the results which ought to be obtained under redistribution, and that in the opinion of those who made presentations the various guidelines were not respected.
There are several guidelines which should be considered by any boundaries commission. Perhaps some of them should be given greater weight than others in a particular situation, but I believe the first guideline which should be followed is an economic one: Does the constituency which is proposed by the boundaries commission have a common or a multiple economic background? Is there a possibility that there is an economic unit within a particular province which comprises a reasonably logical constituency or which can be represented by one individual?
Then we must ask: Are there social guidelines which should be considered? Are there areas which have common points of interest in a social way? Are people acquainted with one another and are they acquainted with one another's interests in a particular area? Do they have something in common, or is there just a conglomeration of people assimilated in a mechanical way without any considera-
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension tion for the knowledge which one group may have of the other in respect of that constituency and its boundaries? Is there any possibility of creating a geographically feasible unit for a member to represent, or is it absolutely necessary that a geographical unit be awkward and difficult to represent, not from the point of view of the member of the House of Commons but from the point of view of the people he represents? How often can they see him in this geographic unit? How often can he call on them? How far does he have to travel? How much of his time is spent on the highway and how much of it is spent in the pursuit of things for his constituents?
These are very important items to the representation of the people but not from the point of view of the members. The member allows his name to go before a convention. He is nominated or he is not. He is either elected or he is not by the people. He has in most instances volunteered; he is not coerced into it. The consideration for the member is not the important subject in this area. The geographic, social and economic possibilities of the people being represented, after they elect the member, is of vital concern.
It is a very high-minded approach to this problem, in the act as we have it, that suggests there should be a nonpolitical approach to the matter of redistribution. There is no way in which you can approach a political problem in a non-political way. There is no way in which somebody who is not familiar with the political intricacies of representation could draw a reasonable constituency boundary in the Dominion of Canada. When you say it shall be non-political, you are denying to the political processes in Canada the reality that political possibilities should be considered.
I like the idea that some people seem to favour, that there is too little non-political discussion in Canada, that everything is based on politics; but I think, in the name of the science of politics, we must give politics proper consideration in the delineation of boundaries. This is not done.
What has occurred has been more a process of gathering groups of people who qualify under the Canada Elections Act into an area delineated by a commission and that is what a constituency is. It has been proven that this act and this concept does not work. Furthermore, I think you have to represent, as the previous speaker pointed out, the rural facets of representation in the House of Commons. I have no quarrel with the fact that somebody who was born and raised in the heart of the city does not understand how to plant an agricultural crop or how to chop down a tree and get it to the mill-I do not understand how to operate a streetcar, and I do not plan to learn-but I think we must take into consideration rural realities as part of the scientific political process in Canada. These people have interests, for instance, in national housing. It is impossible in most instances, and extremely difficult in all, for a housebuilder to obtain money from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation because of the various regulations and guarantees which apply. This is not equitable as far as some citizens in Canada are concerned. The voice to express this need must come from the rural area; it can come from nowhere else, because no one else understands it.
When you take a province of Canada and make its urban areas the focal point of all constituencies, when you say to

July 6, 1973

a province it shall be represented by city representatives, you shall have no rural representation. That is virtually what was said when the province of New Brunswick, except for one or possibly two constituencies, was divided. Then rural life in Canada is not represented in this House. I suggest it would be a disastrous oversight on the part of this House to permit this practice to continue.
I have examined maps of Canada and have found that constituencies in all too many instances radiate from the centres of cities to incorporate rural areas. This renders those areas totally inconsequential in respect of the position a politician will take as he seeks office, because he must approach his constituents in such a fashion as to please the majority of them, and when a rural area becomes a very minor part of a constituency in no way can those people have their voices heard without creating a conflict of interest with the urban part of the constituency. These are principles which I think must be taken into consideration in any redistribution in Canada. The economic guidelines, the social guidelines, the geographic guidelines, the political realities and the rural realities cannot be overlooked.
When it comes to presentations to the commissions, we find that the formality of approach which is required under the act and in the guidelines set down by the commission virtually eliminates some pretty important people in rural Canada who would very much like to express their position in respect of any may as it is drawn. It must be formal, it must be written, and full notice of the guidelines must be laid down in advance. Only one person may speak; there is no opportunity for open discussion at the hearing. This precludes the opportunity for the voter of Canada to express himself as he wishes. If there is any justification for saying that people do not complain about this redistribution, it is because the access of complaint is virtually blockaded by red tape, regulations under the act and by the specific commissions which interpret the act and lay down their own regulations.
The present act is not performing a real service to Canada as a whole. Representation by population is a subject which I am sure can stir up great argument within any party of this House as well as within the House generally. Certainly there was some recognition of the difficulties of rural representation versus urban representation; there was an allowance for a smaller population in some instances. This was to be in recognition of the rural area and a stretching of the ideological representation by population in its literal sense. But as has been pointed out, there are some geographic monstrosities in this country in which there is no possibility for a member of the House of Commons to render to the scattered population the service required and which that population needs as badly or more than the urban population.
I have every sympathy with the ideologies of our democratic people, but I think we have found it is absolutely necessary in virtually every law passed in this country to have certain opportunities for discretion, certain recognition of the realities of the field governed by the individual law, and to have these realities incorporated in any change which is to take place in the electoral boundaries structure of the Dominion of Canada. For instance, there are exam-

pies outside Canada where representation by population is espoused and cherished, yet recognition of vital representation for an area has been contained in all legislation as it has become modernized. The Senate of the United States, for example, has two senators per state regardless of the population of the state. This is intended to give a weighted voice to an area which is sparsely populated but which must have representation.
I think as we consider what we will do about redistribution in this House we must take into consideration both the principle of representation by population and the realities of the capability of a member to serve the needs of his constituency which is scattered over 100,000 miles in the northern part of Manitoba or over half a continent when the Northwest Territories are involved. I believe the people of Canada, if this were explained to them, would be quite willing to accept the realities of geography and to make some sacrifice in order that proper representation will not become a physical impossibility to the member who is elected.
Again I want to make one thing very clear. I am not appealing on my own behalf as a member but on behalf of equitable and capable representation for people. I could not be any more fortunate in respect of the people who live in my constituency. They supported me, they were loyal to me and so far as I know they still are. I respect the opinion of every one of them. However, the failure to recognize the five points I mentioned earlier has put city in with rural, has put a multitude of economic influences into a single constituency and has made it virtually impossible, though it is a great pleasure to try, to give that constituency the representation which it so richly deserves, when a little adjustment to that map of New Brunswick could have recognized the political, social, economic and geographic realities of the province. But they abided by the act: they said, let us get people in bundles in geographic areas and call them constituencies.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think we should go back to the practice of gerrymandering of constituencies. I do not think we should have these ugly-looking prongs of population gathered up into a group of people so that a particular party can win a particular constituency at any given election. I do not recommend that we go back to that, but I do recommend that this act give the House an opportunity to consider the political realities, the political responsibilities and make it possible to construct really practical constituencies in the Dominion of Canada for the representation of people and not for the convenience of members of the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those who question the possibility of getting a consensus on a bill realize now that there may be circumstances-very fortunate indeed- where members recognize that a collective decision should be made in the interest not only of all parties but especially of the Canadian people as a whole.
I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, that the government of which I am member has deemed advisable and urgent to introduce Bill C-208 to suspend the operation of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act.
July 6, 1973

I must admit that like other members I am particularly affected by the report from the Electoral Boundaries Commission.
Indeed if that decision had been implemented, one of the constituencies of the Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean area would have disappeared and the number of federal members in that important area would have dropped from four to three.
The decrease in the number of representatives would be in itself a deplorable consequence of the legislation we wish to pass.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in the Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean area there are five provincial members to meet the people's needs. Conditions were already disturbing for the federal representatives whose number was restricted to four and had a legislation reduced that number to three, it would had been a tragedy.
Not that the federal member for the Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean region refuses to work, nor that he is willing to give his best to meet the needs of the people, but the short time he has and the responsibilities which fall on him prevent him from meeting the people's needs satisfactorily, if the number of his electors and the size of the territory he has to cover make the task impossible.
I find it curious that the Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean region should have been chosen to have a member removed from it. I would very much like to know what reasons were used to justify this absolutely unacceptable choice. Indeed, it is strange that the report gives no justification for this action.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the basic problem which arises in the Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean region, and indeed elsewhere, as was pointed out by my colleague the member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais), is that of representation for rural ridings.
As long as urban and rural ridings are considered on the same footing, we will, in my view, get nowhere.
To assume that the member for a rural riding has the same obligations as the urban member, is to be unrealistic.
As things stand, representation is based on population. Nevertheless I consider this basic principle, though acceptable, to be somewhat faulty.
It seems to me that the principle of proportional representation should be accompanied by basic considerations such as the sociological, psychological and economic factors which, in particular situations, force the member for a rural riding to do a great deal more work than is done in urban ridings.
Of course, I do not wish to offend the members for urban ridings by giving them the impression that we consider our work to be more important. But it is different and requires on the part of members a much more constant presence and much steadier concern for the voters because they carry out their activities in areas remote from large centres where fewer facilities require federal members to have relations often hard to establish since in a certain way they have to be experts in many fields, if not all, and they must be a link between large centres and the communities they represent.
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension
Mr. Speaker, I should like at this point to say quite clearly that the solution we should be considering is not final; I do not pretend to be the one who will propose it to the House but with a bill delaying the implementation of the conclusions in the report we have an opportunity-and I hope we will all avail ourselves of it-to meet frequently in a committee of the House to consider the various aspects of representation at the federal level. I will bare my soul and say that the basic problem as it stands is I think of knowing whether we want federalism to continue to exist. We must decide if we want that federalism which we try to defend and explain to become a way of helping the people and the principle of federalism to continue to exist, particularly in Quebec.
If we reduce representation we will be the ones to blame if Canada faces additional difficulties. The basic problem is simply of knowing whether we want Canada with its differences of opinions and basic problems with respect to federalism, to solve its problems or let them worsen.
I will try to make my comments quite simple and indicate to hon. members, to all Canadians and to the people of the Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean area that I am deeply concerned by the proposed solution aimed at eliminating one member from the Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean area. Therefore, I welcome this bill introduced by the government and with the support of all parties, I believe it will give us an opportunity to make a thorough appraisal of federalism and the rights of citizens to be adequately represented in the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, I do not suggest that it would be advisable to push for a much larger representation since we must draw the line somewhere and keep in mind some basic principles, as the right of rural ridings to be represented in the House not necessarily according to the number of voters, but according to their rights, their responsibilities, their real needs which are often more difficult to meet than in urban ridings where adequate services are available.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the delay proposed in this bill will enable us to find proper, just and reasonable solutions to that problem. The Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean area will thus keep all its members so that they will be in a position to give better service, as we are always willing to do provided this House takes its responsibilities and avoids the mistake of decreasing the number of rural members, especially in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area, who have a great part to play and are prepared to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the introduction of a bill to suspend the operation of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) strikes me as being a rather classic example of what in the British tradition is known as muddling through. I suppose we are going to muddle through this particular exercise, although it is obvious to me, from having listened to the debate so far, that in effect we have opened up quite a can of worms. It is a little difficult to consider what the real principle of the bill is because, as the President of the Privy Council said, it is an operation to stop the clock.

July 6, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension
One of the aspects of the matter which the minister touched upon, and which has not been mentioned too much by recent speakers, is the particular conundrum which results from an apparent oversight in the original Electoral Boundaries Act as to there being a period of time when it would be obviously impossible for an election to be held. In the situation of a parliament such as this, where an election could occur unexpectedly, it might be virtually impossible-this has been suggested-to hold an election for up to 12 months. The people of Canada would be denied the opportunity to exercise their basic right to vote for that length of time.
If one thinks of the matter in those terms one can see that all the President of the Privy Council needed to do was to introduce a bill to amend section 23 of the act. That is one of the important considerations before us. One could probably argue that that is the only consideration we need to have before us, because I recall that consideration of the original bill on this matter seemed to cover all possibilities in regard to ensuring that an election could be held at any time on one set of boundaries or the other, but later it became apparent that in the context of the immediate situation this was not possible. If in fact a previous parliament created a situation in which it would be impossible to hold an election for a period of up to a year following dissolution of parliament, that is a situation which was not anticipated and it is certainly one that cannot continue. If that were all that concerned the President of the Privy Council, we probably could have had quick and easy passage of that proposition.
Possibly some members who come from certain provinces-reference has already been made to British Columbia from which I come-could say that that is all that really needs to be done, that that is the decision that should be made, and if circumstances dictate that an election be held before the new boundaries are established we would be willing to hold it on the basis of the old boundaries. In effect, this is an easy position for a member to take, a member who represents a province that stands to gain seats under the current redistribution process, and my first inclination was to say that that was all we needed to do; why should we get into all this tangle that is being developed? But, Mr. Speaker, the bill has opened up many other questions far beyond those which were set forth by the President of the Privy Council.
Obviously, some members are using this bill as an opportunity to discuss the actions of the redistribution commissions within their provinces. Two or three hon. members have forcefully argued that the commissions should suspend their operations. I am not sure that I agree with them, because if this bill were not before us, if it did not pass, we would have an opportunity under the old arrangement, under the terms of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, to debate those very questions when dealing with the objections filed by members to the various redistribution proposals. From that point of view I would argue that the bill, in the context that some members see it, is unnecessary.
In view of the remarks that have been made in relation to the actions of some of the commissions it might be well to remind members, particularly those who were not here

at the time the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act was brought into being, of the provisions of that act, dealing with the terms of reference of the commissions, debating whether they were being followed in the spirit that parliament intended and considering whether some revision might need to be made. The basic debate that took place when the act was introduced was on the question of representation by population versus geographic size, something which has been much to the fore in the remarks of some hon. members. I think there was general agreement on the basic premise that all citizens' votes should have the same weight in choosing who would represent them in this House, but there was recognition that in a country the size of Canada this was not completely practicable or, indeed, in some respects fair.
The act allows for a maximum difference of 50 per cent, so that in effect it is possible for the weight of an urban vote to be only half the weight of a vote cast in a large, sparsely populated constituency. I am reasonably satisfied with the work that was done by the redistribution commission in British Columbia, because while it did not in any case go to the extreme of 50 per cent up and down from the average, according to my analysis it did go to quite an extent in recognizing the geographic factor for which provision is made in the act, and generally speaking the larger the riding the smaller is the population. This may or may not be the case in some of the other provinces. I have not examined them in great detail and I really do not know the constituency boundaries well enough in other provinces to feel capable of examining them in any depth.
However, I suggest that newer members should give careful thought to the position they are taking because they may be faced with a difficult alternative. The hon. member from New Brunswick who spoke recently said he did not want to go back to the gerrymandering type of redistribution performed in the past by committees of this House. There are not many members of the present House who went through that process. I myself have not been here long enough to go through that exercise. I see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) looking in my direction. In fact he referred to this matter in his remarks. He remembers the kind of agony that was involved.

speechtext: I went through it twice and it was real agony.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
The hon. member says that he went through it twice and it was real agony. I suggest that hon. members should think about those words. If some hon. members are suggesting that in effect we should abandon the principles of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, or if they are suggesting that we should go beyond the 50 per cent up and down presently permissible, what is the alternative but to go back to having the readjustment done by a parliamentary committee, with all the dangers of log-rolling that it would involve? Some of us can remember hearing about all that in times past and in fact some of us became quite aware of the results of that process. In my submission it was one of the black marks on our democracy. It meant that the party in power at any particular time had an opportunity to influence the boundaries of constituencies in a way that would be favourable to its chances of retaining office following a general elec-
July 6, 1973

tion. I hope we have permanently turned our backs on that practice in this parliament.
Some hon. members have talked about the difficulties of representing large geographic areas with scattered populations. Reference has also been made to the situation in the United States with respect to the composition of the U.S. Senate. There may be reason for us to think about some of the things that go on in that regard. I suggest something that I do not think has been mentioned and, if I understand correctly, is recognized in the United States in relation to the operation of their Senate. Although each state is represented by two senators, it is recognized that different senators carry different workloads and provision is made for a differential in staffing, which enables those senators to cope with their workloads and problems.
Actually, the question of members' staffs has already been raised in this debate, quite legitimately. If one thinks in terms of serving a constituency and dealing with the needs of people living in sparsely populated and remote communities, one will see that that question is not unrelated to the question of redistribution and the manner in which seats are established. In my view, that would be a more fruitful course for us to pursue as opposed to any attempt to go further than the present act permits. I am speaking of the differential in the voting weight of certain people. It would be better if we could provide more adequate staff for members so that a member could provide the kind of service to people in remote and small communities that was mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) in his speech last night.
The work of the redistribution commissions or the matter of the re-evaluation of the concepts in the existing act really did not form the basis of the remarks of the President of the Privy Council. That was not his rationale for suggesting that we should suspend the operation of the act. If I understood him correctly, he suggested that in this interval of suspended operation of the act we must look, really, at the constitutional position of this House, that is to say, the distribution of members as between the various provinces of Canada. That question in not unrelated to the one concerning sparsely populated and remote constituencies. That, really, is the key question that the government and the President of the Privy Council are asking us to consider in seeking support for this bill. This argument has been made by some members from provinces which stand to lose seats, which are in an unfair position in relation to other provinces because of the so-called senatorial floor. This is the rationale which has been put forward in this debate.
I agree, although I am reluctant to do so, coming as I do from British Columbia, that perhaps this is the question with which we should be concerned. Perhaps this is something which can be accomplished in the present parliament. It might be more difficult to accomplish in a parliament differently structured. I remind the President of the Privy Council through you, Mr. Speaker, that the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act was passed by a minority parliament which set up the principle of having the process carried out by commissions. This matter has been ignored for a long time by various majority parliaments. I could argue that the right hon. member for Prince Albert
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension (Mr. Diefenbaker) and any other member who is concerned about a province losing members could have done this in the previous parliament. The effect of the previous redistribution made as apparent as the proposals of the present redistribution the inequities in the distribution of members as between provinces.
It would be easy for someone like me to say, "Why did you not raise this question in the last parliament and get it over with? We would have had in operation a fairer system of distribution. Why come along now and ask members from provinces which are likely to gain fairer representation in the House to stop the clock? If an election could be held beyond the point at which it would be feasible after the new boundaries are in operation, why ask members to retain their existing position which is unfair in relation to the total population of the country?" I could say that should have been done in the previous parliament. On the other hand, I am rather doubtful whether the President of the Privy Council, as government House leader, would have paid as much attention to arguments along those lines in the last parliament as he is paying to them now. Then he sat beside a Prime Minister who commanded a reasonable majority in the House.
I am inclined to say, "A particular set of circumstances has created an opportunity, and we are prepared to take a real look at the constitutional distribution of seats as between provinces." If the President of the Privy Council really means what he says, that he is going to make sure we come to grips with this problem, and if I understood him correctly we shall do so later this session, and if I can be satisfied that there will be a serious opportunity to come to grips with this question which, when coupled with the amending provision will ensure that there is no hiaitus, then on reflection I think this might be a fruitful operation.
I believe it is one o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I wish to make a few more remarks on this matter when we resume.
At one o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned for lunch I had just touched upon the fact that the President of the Privy Council had indicated, as his justification for bringing in this bill to suspend the operations of redistribution, the need for us to have a new look at the whole question of the distribution of seats between our various provinces and the manner in which that works out under the present constitutional arrangements. I had suggested this perhaps might be the kind of parliament in which something could be worked out. It would open up a whole new approach in this area. If in fact it was the intention of the President of the Privy Council that this be a serious job for parliament, there might be some justification for this process. We could argue, of course, that the process could go on and do in fact what he has suggested in this bill. That, of course, is the other side of the coin.
5376

July 6, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension
I think the time is ripe to look at the basic arrangements for deciding how many seats the various provinces will have. In this connection, I have in my hand a copy of a map originally published by the surveys and mapping branch in 1967. It is entitled "Territorial Evolution of Canada from 1667 to 1949." I recommend this map to hon. members because it reveals interesting aspects of the way in which Canada as we know it today came into being. Presumably in 1949, with the accession of Newfoundland, we reached the end of territorial evolution for the foreseeable future. This may be some justification for taking a new look at the situation.
Throughout the whole of our history, parliament has been faced with this conundrum posed by geography and population density. The arrangements now in existence represent an attempt to solve that question. The fact is that arrangements which were useful and necessary in 1867 do not necessarily apply today, and that some of the ad hoc arrangements which were entered upon in earlier years have become increasingly unrealistic.
If one looks at this map one recognizes that in succeeding parliaments over a long period there has always been a certain amount of give and take in our federal state in an effort to work out something which would be generally fair and acceptable. One of the small maps on the sheet shows the territorial situation as it was in 1873, the year in which the province of Prince Edward Island entered confederation-as we have all been made aware in recent weeks. In the immediately preceding period the fifth and sixth provinces had entered confederation, Manitoba in 1870 and British Columbia in 1871. One thing which struck me immediately when I looked at this map was that in 1872, British Columbia having recently acceded, the area of that province represented roughly 50 per cent of the total area of Canada contained within the boundaries of the provinces. This may come as a shock to members from Ontario and Quebec who are used to thinking in terms of the present boundaries of those provinces. This is a good example of the kind of give and take which existed, because when British Columbia entered confederation it was agreed that the province should have six seats in the Commons and six seats in the Senate. Its population, for this purpose, was deemed to be about 60,000.
I have not done research on this aspect of the matter but I assume that MPs then sitting in this chamber represented roughly 10,000 electors. The existence of the Indian population was disregarded at that time; they were not considered to be "persons" for election purposes. Recognition was given to the fact that here was a whole new area coming into confederation, roughly doubling the size of the area within provincial boundaries, and it was decided that British Columbia should be entitled to a minimum of six seats, even though its actual population was only 10 or 12 thousand. Prince Edward Island, which came into confederation a year later, was given four seats. Prince Edward Islanders may be aware of the Island's population at that time, but I would estimate that the population might then have been in the vicinity of 40,000. In other words, their representation approximated the population basis and the question of the size of the province was disregarded.

I represent a constituency which is not one of the larger ones in British Columbia. Nevertheless, it is roughly half the size of the province from which the President of the Privy Council comes. You could put Prince Edward Island in the middle of my constituency and not be much more than aware of its presence. Yet, as I say, my constituency is not one of the larger in British Columbia. I am pointing out that throughout our history recognition has been given to circumstances of this kind. Consideration has been given to what is described in the legislation as special geographical factors including, in particular, the population density or relative rates of growth of the various regions and the special community or diversity of interest of the inhabitants of those regions. No one would quarrel with the suggestion that in a federal state the inhabitants of a province share a special community of interest.
In my view, any serious revaluation of this process must begin with recognition that the existing basic provision in the constitution about the relationship of the number of members sent by a province to this place with the number of Senators from a province, is outmoded and unrealistic today. If it is felt we should take a rational look at the composition of the other place, this would involve a radical revision of the number of senators there. However, I submit this ought to be considered as a separate question.
I like the suggestion put forward by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre that we could achieve a worthwhile purpose, for example in relation to Prince Edward Island, of not decreasing its membership in the House if we were to adopt a formula to provide that a province could be entitled to one member for each 25,000 of population up to, say, the first 100,000. After that point, the number of members from a province would decrease in relation to total population. A formula of this kind would remedy a situation which is of obvious concern to members representing provinces such as Manitoba and Saskatchewan. It would also help answer the conundrum which perpetually faces provinces such as New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, at least if their populations do not change greatly.
I should like to point out, too, that though we have probably reached the limit of our territorial evolution we have not yet reached the limit of what I might call our constitutional evolution. I have in mind the territories of Canada which between them embrace more than one-third of the total geographic area of our country. I think there is some validity to the argument, if one has in mind a situation parallel to that in respect of British Columbia when it entered confederation, dealing with vast geographic areas. Any new formula must recognize the principle enunciated in the boundaries readjustment act. The principle to which I refer has been used in the case of the territories where the population is deemed to be somewhat larger for the purposes of representation in this House.
Apart from the question involving the territories and the problems that will develop when they attain provincial status, I suggest our constitutional framework is pretty well complete, at least in so far as the immediate issues of this House are concerned. There is always the possibility of union between provinces, but- we need not concern ourselves with that at the moment.
July 6, 1973

The time has come to take a whole new look at the question of drafting a bill which would prevent representation decreasing in the provinces, while at the same time removing the increasing inequities which have developed in relation to the number of members in this House and the number of members in the other place. If we can come to serious grips with this problem in an expeditious way, then perhaps we will not delay the redistribution process. We will then not be thinking in terms of two or three elections on the basis of the present electoral boundaries in the provinces and the same number of seats. If that can be done, I think this will be worth-while exercise.
When the President of the Privy Council introduced the bill I think he was deliberately vague and did not give us concrete ideas in respect of what the government thought we might do during this exercise. He said the government would be putting some proposals before us. But I think it would be worth while, having listened to the discussion, if before this debate ends the President of the Privy Council would be more specific regarding the approach, approaches, the alternative or alternatives that should be taken, without transgressing the normal rule about giving details of a bill before its presentation.
This general exercise involves all of us as members of parliament. I think the President of the Privy Council will agree that although he may be proposing the bill on behalf of the government, basically he will be proposing it as a member of parliament who happens to occupy a particular position in the scheme of things at this point of our history and it should be considered carefully. I feel we must take the time to develop an idea of how we should arrive at appropriate redistribution, and we should at the time consider how over the last 100 years we have arrived at our present position. Perhaps we should remember the give and take which has existed at various points in time during the course of our territorial evolution, and bear in mind as well the rapid growth which has taken place in our population during this accelerated trend since the end of World War II.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was quite impressed by some of the sensible remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), especially those in respect of section 23 of the act which is now to be emasculated. Bill C-208 will likely prove to be one of the most disgraceful pieces of legislation to come before this House. This legislation says to some Canadians: You are entitled to two, three, four, five or even eight times more say in the affairs of this country than other Canadians who happen to live in growing, burgeoning urban areas of Canada.
This legislation says to Canadians in these burgeoning areas of Canada: Because you are productive and your communities are growing, because you happen to live in new homes and apartments, you do not rate. That is too bad, because some members of this House who come from small ridings want to protect their establishments, their preferred positions and their communities. The powers are suggesting, through this legislation, that those who support this bill are in favour of the concept that fairness does not matter, that representation by population does not
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension matter and be damned to those things. They are saying that the large ridings must be protected.
The Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act was passed a short time ago and was intended to protect against gerrymandering and to give some strength to the concept of representation by population. It was intended to give Canadians generally protection against the kind of thing now being presented to the House of Commons in this bill introduced by the President of the Privy Council. I say to you and to this House, Mr. Speaker, that all Canadians are equal; there are no Canadians who are entitled to two, three or even eight voices; all Canadians should have an equal voice in the management of the affairs of this country.
There are monstrous changes taking place in the world. People are moving from the farms and rural areas to the cities in all parts of this world. There are more people in Canada today than in 1961 and, indeed, in 1867. We must expect more changes. When looking at the records in connection with representation in this House, I discovered that in the election following the entry of Prince Edward Island to confederation that island had six seats on the basis of representation by population. One can see from this that there have been massive changes in population. If my riding had representation on the basis of population as it existed in respect of Prince Edward Island, there would be eight members representing Peel South in this House.
In 1961 my area was a township with a population of about 75,000. In 1968 it became a town, and on January 1, 1974, it will become the city of Mississauga. That town presently has a population in excess of 200,000, probably 215,000. The growth rate is such that more people are moving in every year than lived in the Northwest Territories at the time of the last election. On the basis of representation by population, according to the 1971 census, my city of Mississauga is entitled to two members in this House of Commons. It is entitled to two votes on matters which come before this House of Commons. It is entitled to two ombudsmen to answer the problems of the people who live in my city. It is entitled to two offices for members and it is entitled to constituency help on the basis of twice what it is getting today. That is on the basis of the 1971 census which, with the growth rate of my city, is totally wrong; none the less, it is on the basis of the 1971 census.
With the present growth rate, assuming ridings in this country were to stay approximately the same size, by 1981 as a result of a redistribution following that census my city may well be entitled to four representatives in this House. Yet the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), coming from a riding that is likely to disappear as a result of redistribution, proposes that one of his people is entitled to three times the vote of a person who comes from my city of Mississauga at the present time, and that ratio is likely to become worse and worse. The result of this particular bill is that we could well have another federal election and a parliament lasting to 1978 or 1979 and the inequities could become greater and greater. I have been asked by members of my party not to speak out because some of them are worried about their seats.

speechtext:
I have been asked by members on the other side not to speak out because they are worried about their seats. But I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I am concerned about my people in Mississauga. I think they are entitled to a fair shake and are entitled to be heard. My people are already entitled at this time to two members in the House of Commons. Are they expected to settle for one member in the House of Commons until 1981 or longer?
If this bill should be passed, is it not possible for this House of Commons, controlled perhaps by members with much seniority coming from smaller ridings, to again insist on another delay in redistribution because, after all, we might as well wait until the results of the 1981 census, and after that another census, and so the whole question of representation by population would be thrown in a cocked hat? In the name of fairness, this bill should not be proceeded with. It should fail.
Much has been said in this chamber and outside about the activities of the provincial commissions in dealing with arrangements within each province for the distribution of seats in the province. When the first map came out dividing the town of Mississauga it did not present a realistic breakdown of the town along communication lines within the town. As a result of representations made by the town and by the two major political parties-the NDP could not bother-the commission paid attention to the requirements of the people living in the town and made a division of the ridings to which Mississauga is entitled into two proper, distinct sections. No one wants to see his town divided. No one wants to see his town underrepresented either. So that division took place and I commend the commission for a job well done in the province of Ontario. I suggest that commissions in other provinces probably would have done a more satisfactory job had the members from those provinces made sure they were properly represented before the commission and had done something about what they describe as inequities. Those inequities could have been corrected if they had paid attention to their job.
As a member coming from Ontario and having talked to other members from the province, I can say that the commission in that province did a fair job so far as possible in making apportionments of the province to take into account geography and to some extent to take into account transportation and sociological factors. The commission came up with what can be described only as "well done".
Some members have said that the number of members in this House should be increased to 300. That supposedly would protect people. But we know, of course, that once we increase the number of members to 300 and our population increases, we eventually would have to change this chamber around completely. We really would not accomplish very much in that way. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that a member of parliament with the proper tools, with the proper constituency offices and with the proper secretarial help to handle the job-as suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni-if he should have a large geographic constituency perhaps should be given extra travel money. Some of the activities of the Treasury Board in respect of the House of Commons budget today

discriminate against the use of air travel for getting around a riding, and against help for riding offices. This makes the problem of communication enormously expensive and exceedingly difficult. If this could be resolved, it would solve many of the concerns of members with large ridings. However, there is no particular reason why this House of Commons should be expanded just to protect the peculiar vested interest of some members, and I include the right hon. member from Prince Albert, to keep their seats.
It is about time we had a rethink in this country. If we are to start attacking representation by population, perhaps we should attack some of the other vestiges of protectionism which exist under the British North America Act. Is there anything really inviolate about provincial boundaries? Just because provinces entered confederation as a group, is there anything that says their boundaries and limitations are sacrosanct? If the province of Saskatchewan and the province of Manitoba are losing seats, are losing population and are losing vitality, is there any reason why they could not talk about amalgamating? The same might apply to the provinces of the Atlantic region. Is there any reason why an island of perhaps 120,000 people should be represented by four members in this House of Commons, other than the fact that it has been a province for 100 years?
If we are to start talking about the fact that representation by population is not proper, let us attack the real problem. The real problem may be that some people in this country because of history say they have a vested interest, and I suggest they have not. Members from Saskatchewan and Newfoundland do not want to talk about preserving their present over-representation.

speechtext: Give them Ottawa East.

I for one want to talk about the real justification for their maintaining in different provinces, when I look at the amounts of money transferred by the federal government to those provinces, separate institutions, from county courts to supreme courts, to special Senate seats. I think we must recognize this.
Some hon. members think that because they represent a great deal of territory in Canada their constituencies should have more than one representative in this House. I refer to the bill presently before the House introduced by the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth). I say that he represents a territory equal to about one-third of the size of Canada, but I also say that he does not represent the tundra, he does not represent trees and rocks and he does not represent territory. He represents people. I, also, do not represent pavement, apartments, office buildings and airport runways. I represent people. We represent citizens in this country, we represent voters. We come here as their delegates. We are the delegates of people, not of acres of land, of square miles, of hundreds of miles of shoreline and that kind of thing. We are here to represent Canadians.
Just because our system divides groups of Canadians into constituencies which allows those groups to pick representatives and makes possible a voting system does
July 6, 1973

not mean, under any circumstances, that you represent a territory that is your feifdom or your seignory. I do not represent the town of Mississauga or the town council; I happen to represent Canadians who live in the riding of Peel South. Those Canadians pay taxes to Ottawa. Some of them who live in the riding of Peel South earn their living in other parts of Canada, in other ridings, and they have interests in those ridings. Some of those Canadians have summer cottages in other ridings and investment in the Northwest Territories, in ridings in the province of Quebec and the province of New Brunswick.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the oil in the province of Alberta does not just belong to Albertans or to people who say they are Albertans. It belongs to Canadians. I happen to represent Canadians who come from the riding of Peel South, and the members from Alberta represent Canadians who come from ridings in the province of Alberta. But they all have interests in other parts of Canada, because Canada has a whole identity. What we must remember is that our ridings are not feifdoms and are not duchies. We are not here only to make it possible for Canadians as citizens of this country to vote on a representative basis, to have a representative in the House of Commons on a population basis to represent them in debates.
It has been said that we should talk about territory. I could talk about territory if I wanted to do so, but I will not speak on that matter. My territory is still pretty big. It is nearly half the size of the city of Toronto. We could talk just as easily about the principle of no taxation without representation. We could introduce another feature into representation in this House. We could talk about the principle that if you pay taxes you get votes, and we could talk about how much taxes are paid. We could talk about the fact that the great golden horseshoe area pays about half the taxes that we spend-or squander, as the case may be-in the House of Commons. If we talk about taxation without representation, we might as well and as easily talk about half the members of the House of Commons coming from the golden horseshoe area. That would be just as sensible as talking about the fact that Ellesmere Island is a huge territory and perhaps should have an additional member of parliament.
I will not suggest to the House the principle of representation on the basis of taxation, but if I did suggest it it could well work out that my riding would have as many members in the House as the provinces of Newfoundland and New Brunswick put together.

We do not represent people on the basis of the land that they happen to occupy. Nor do we consider that they are better because they happen to come from a rural area, or because their fathers or their grandfathers owned that farm. We represent Canadians because they are all Canadians and they are all entitled to an equal say in Canada. No one is a better Canadian because he happens to come from an established community, and that is the sense of the bill that is presently before us. That is the sense of some of the arguments that have been presented in favour of the bill. People in my constituency may rent an apartment or a room; they may move from my constituency to a neighbouring one many times. The number of
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension people in my constituency can change rapidly and the names of the people will change rapidly.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext: I hope not.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Some of the people in my constituency will not be there next week or next month. The only reason we have constituencies is to make it possible at the time of an election for people to vote. My people pay taxes to this government. They are not worried about the fact that those taxes go to protect the outraged parts of this country. They are not worried about the fact that transportation schemes are used without care as to how many people are there, but to tie this country together because they own parts of this country and they recognize that they are part of it. They want to be part of it. One of the problems suggested is that they do not care about the outraged parts of this country. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that they certainly do.
The activities of the leadership of the province of Ontario before dominion-provincial conferences clearly indicate that the province of Ontario has always cared about Canada and has given leadership. It has certainly given better leadership than has this government across the aisle. It is time we got rid of the idea that some people are entitled to be discriminated against because they come from cities. It is time we recognized that while democracy does not just mean representation by population, this principle is an essential feature of any democracy.
It is time to throw out this bill that is designed to preserve inequities. A great deal of attention was given to the present act which allows for a decennial redistribution of the electoral boundaries. Basically it is a good act. There is a problem, however, in that it may be difficult to call an election at a certain time as a result of the dissolution of parliament. A minor amendment allowing an overlap period until the establishment of the new constituency boundaries, allowing use of the old boundaries until the new boundaries could be reorganized in the field, would not be at all wrong. But we do not have to throw out the baby with the bathwater.
It is time we recognized the fact that Canadians are equal. There is no superior Canadian because he comes from a rural area, and no inferior Canadian because he comes from a city. All Canadians are working to build one Canada, to build a better Canada-and we will not build a better Canada, an equitable Canada, a great Canada by discrimination and discriminatory practices.

speechtext:
My point is that the hon. member who finished his speech, in calling for a reduction of the seats that would be available to a province like Alberta is trying to open the door to rape Alberta in the same way as the province of Ontario and the city of Toronto have raped northwestern Ontario. Regional representation is part of the essence of what we are discussing in this bill.
A formula based solely and strictly on representation by population is not realistic in Canadian terms. This country was not put together that way. The historic dynamics of this country militate against that kind of operation. If the hon. member bothers to read Hansard he will find that many people on his side of the House take the same view of Canadian history as do those of us on this side. I sincerely hope, for the good of Canada, that he is a voice crying in the wilderness.
When we are dealing with parliamentary representation we must deal with the two problems that are covered in this bill. The first is the problem of overlapping. If this bill does not pass we will end up with a situation, given that the parties are so precariously balanced in this House, that it would not be possible for us to have an election for a year. Obviously, that is an intolerable situation.
The second point is that the operation of the present act does not provide sufficient flexibility to ensure that regions in Canada will be able to maintain a vestige of the position which it is important for them to have. In other words, we on this side of the House recognize that the economic, taxation and social policies followed by the Government of Canada and the larger provinces can and do have a significant effect on the distribution of population, a significant influence on the way in which wealth is distributed and a significant impact on the economic potentialities of any particular region. That surely, is a factor that has to be taken into consideration when a redistribution bill is developed.
The other point I want to make is that the existing act has significant defects in it, some of which were observable in the first instance in 1965 and which I believe have been shown to be substantially confirmed in a way that the original drafters of the act had not anticipated. Take, for example, the provision to provide a 25 per cent leeway between ridings in a province. There are some provinces where the 25 per cent has been used. There are other provinces where no leeway was used. Surely this is tremendously unfair both between regions in provinces and between provinces. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the act as it has been interpreted by the various commissions had not been logical, has not been reasonable; therefore it has to be changed.

There is a problem involved in the distribution of seats as among provinces. We do have a very great range of the powers and the abilities of the provinces within Canada. No one can deny this. A province like Prince Edward Island is a province not like the others. It is small; it has a very small population. Yet it is entitled to be represented by four members in this House. But P.E.I. was one of the originals in terms of the negotiation of confederation: it joined in 1873. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick also have special positions in confederation as original participants in the federation of 1867. So, Mr. Speaker, we have a whole series of historic precedents bound up in the history of Canada which we cannot ignore and which, if we do ignore, we do so at our peril.
The purpose of this bill is to ensure two things. The first is that we do not end up in a situation where an election is called and we cannot have one. I believe all hon. members will accept that that is a problem which must be dealt with. Secondly, the bill attempts to deal with the problem of the inefficiencies in the act and the way in which seats are distributed across Canada both as between provinces and as between regions within provinces. It is important to emphasize that this is not going to be an easy matter, and so the bill provides for an interruption of the process for only 18 months.
If the government and the political parties are unable to come up with a satisfactory solution, then the bill will lapse and the existing boundaries, after consultation with reconstituted provincial commissions and the holding of hearings, again will proceed forward. So it is our responsibility to come up with an alternative to the system we have.
The current redistribution act is less than eight years old. It has been used effectively only once. We have discovered a great many objections to the way in which it operates. We have discovered it does not take into consideration all of the dynamics of our contry. We shall have to have discussions among ourselves, particularly among members of all parties, to develop another act. Whether this new act will involve the creation of additional seats in the House of Commons or whether it will develop some other formula to distribute seats among provinces and regions is not for me to say.
I want to deal with one other point. It concerns the problem which I and a number of other members share with the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth). We represent vast geographical regions in Canada with scattered populations throughout them. There are no major centres, no large cities; there is a series of rather small centres. Given the existing structure of parliament and the existing powers of a member of parliament, it is simply impossible for a member adequately to serve these areas.
To make the matter even worse, doing all the things the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) suggested, such as taking on extra staff and opening constituency offices, would not be adequate. Many remote communities are not served adequately with telephones, do not have adequate highways and communications networks. Most of them are still seeking the basic services which people in

larger metropolitan centres take for granted. It is impossible for a member of parliament representing a large regional riding to deal adequately with 44, 45, or 50 municipalities, all of which have problems and all of which come to the member of parliament for assistance in dealing with them.
We need more time to get our and make a circuit of these areas. We cannot do this now, with the way parliament operates at present. With the explosion in government services and in legislation that has come about in the last few years, piling more and more work on the shoulders of the member of parliament, our opportunity for servicing these areas properly is diminishing. Perhaps in future parliaments members who represent large rural ridings will need to decide whether, as members of parliament, they will participate in the activities of this House or devote their time almost exclusively to serving the requirements of their ridings. One cannot do both any more; it once used to be possible. So in arriving at any solution to this problem, we must take into account the fact that there are people up among the rocks, the trees and the tundra who have a right to be adequately represented.
It is a principle of fundamental importance that every citizen should have access to his member of parliament. It is far more difficult for the 60,000 people I represent to have access to me than it is for the people of an urban riding to have access to their member of parliament. He is available, but the member of parliament representing a large rural riding is simply not available to the same extent, by definition. It strikes me, when we talk about a Canada that is to grow and about providing equal service to citizens, that we are talking not only about a formula that will provide for representation on the basis of population but, as well, about a formula giving each citizen access to his member of parliament and the government of Canada. If that does not happen I submit all the rhetoric of the hon. member for Peel South will remain just that, sheer rhetoric, sheer bull!
