Mr. Speaker, as do most hon. members, I believe that it was quite in order for Bill C-208 to be brought before us, not with a view to delaying the application of new electoral boundaries indefinitely, but simply in order to complete the work of the Electoral Boundaries Commission for the province of Quebec, which is now only in draft form.
For example, if we examine the proposed readjustment of the boundaries of the large riding of Portneuf, which I have the honour to represent, one says to oneself: there are two possibilities: the diagram was drawn either by kindergarten children, or by adults used to making the least effort, and who have tried to draw zigzags resembling forked lightning. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the proposed new boundaries for the riding of Portneuf avoid cities and, in some cases, divide municipalities. The present population of Portneuf is 125,000, far larger than that of Prince Edward Island. Yet the present boundaries of the riding which I have the honour to represent have existed only since 1968.
That is why I say that the report of the members of the commission is just another report and that the members of
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension this commission are just like the members of other commissions, that is they stop forwards, then backwords and end up in the same place. Once again we have an example of an organization which is of no benefit to the public.
Some ridings are having municipalities added on. Others, are having them removed. And in my opinion, whether the unemployed are in one riding or another, whether the students wait for their grants in one riding or another, whether businesses go bankrupt in one riding or another, things won't change very much, little matter what happens after the project is implemented. What they are proposing, more or less, is to displace the boundaries of some ridings and even, in some cases, to move whole ridings. Actually, it is not because a house has been moved that it is more comfortable.
Altogether, this bill merely requests the House to agree to postpone application of another bill which is not beneficial to the people.
Mr. Speaker, it goes without saying that I am completely in favour of getting rid of a mini reform, but I am all for a true reform that would bring results.
All things considered, Canadians are the taxpayers and are entitled to results.
Since the government now deals with everything and goes through everybody's pockets, it is obvious that as members of Parliament we must answer an increasing number of requests, either as regards unemployment insurance or tax matters. We must deal with young people seeking scholarships or other people who experience difficulties with old age pension, family allowances, winter works, expended credit, Opportunities for youth and New Horizons Programs, employment applications, welfare benefit requests, expropriations related to CFB Valcartier or Mirabel airport, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, postal service, public works, passports, the admission of elder people in homes, the release of prisoners, farm credit, combined retirement pensions of Crown corporations, excise and sales taxes, grants to industries, workmen compensation, work permits, vocational training, military transfers, railway crossings, closing-down of railway stations and repairs to fences of farmers living close to CN lines.
Those are all matters, Mr. Speaker, which lead our constituents to consult us; it may happen that workmen, for instance, are asked to pay a tax which is not justified at all and then we must plead their case. Or else unemployed people must sometimes wait for three or four months to receive benefits; then they must fight against defective computers that refuse to accept payments to which these people are entitled under another legislation.
And so it is within the whole federal administration, Mr. Speaker. Portneuf, the riding that I have the honour to represent, is served by two Unemployment Insurance Commission offices. One is located in Quebec City and the other in Trois-Rivieres.
As for the income tax problems, we can deal for a while with the Quebec City local office, but sooner or later we must go to the source and often apply to the Montreal regional office.

As far as social welfare allowances are concerned, which in Quebec are shared equally by the federal government, my constituency is covered by three offices, one in Char-lesbourg, another in Donnacona and the third in Quebec City.
The proposed boundaries in the notorious report change absolutely nothing to the conditions since, even if the report as submitted was passed, we would have to continue to work with the two unemployment insurance offices to which I referred. As for social welfare, we would also continue to work with the three offices which I have just mentioned.
I agree, Mr. Speaker, with the principle of the bill that all members should represent about the same population.
However, I hardly think it is necessary to change the electoral boundaries if we are not doing anything to improve the services to which the people are entitled. At present, as previous speakers have pointed out, there are days when Members of Parliament should be in three different places at the same time.
First of all, they must be in the House to take part in the debates; this is the first reason why they have been elected. Second, on the same day, many members must attend sittings of committees and at the same time remain in their respective ridings or go to the nearest town to make a plea concerning some services of some departments.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, it is normal that the member of parliament should support the people who face problems created by the present government. However, to meet adequately the demands of the people, to get tangible results, it is urgent to think about setting up additional services.
Concerning these services, I am pleased to call again for the establishment of what we have already asked for in this House, namely the organization of an office in each riding and the help of a secretary. All departmental offices and those of all government commissions are open only five days a week, the same as those when the House is sitting and all members must be present. It is obvious that a man or woman employed in an office in a riding would have a great role to fulfil.
I think that these persons could become advisers to help people avail themselves of the government services available at various levels.
Unfortunately, until now everyone has had to act in a happy-go-lucky manner, always taking a chance when applying to the Unemployment Insurance Commission or an income tax office whose forms have become like traps since they have been designed by experts always ready to embarrass everyone. But I think that there is a growing need for someone working within the ridings to help people-benefit from all the advantages available.
Yet, over the last ten years, the Canadian government has established about 50 royal commissions of inquiry charged with studying all kinds of matters, all kinds of circumstances. At the end, we are still waiting for results, but I think that we.know very well the present situation in respect of the voters' claims, and I think that it is time to take action.

Setting up an office in each riding to enable the member to stay in contact with the citizens would be, to my mind, an efficient and inexpensive step, compared with some of the questionable initiative taken by the present government.
As the present bill suggests very little to increase the services expected by the citizens, I urge the minister who pilots the bill to take advantage of the extension to be granted by Bill C-208 to draft a bill providing the indispensable and positive measure's which all taxpayers demand.
I also take this opportunity to suggest to the minister that a revision of the constitution be made not only to increase the number of members but to achieve it.
As municipalities and cities develop, as the population grows, I feel that we must act as businessmen. When the customers grow in number, there is but one thing to do: increase the number of salesmen.
Let us therefore quit going around in circles, let us make plans and act to really help the population and meet their wishes. They pay the bill and are therefore entitled to what they request.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words on Bill C-208 which will suspend the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act until December 31, 1974 and provide an opportunity to reassess the situation in Canada with regard to reasonable representation in our parliament.
It was the duty of the commissions concerned to readjust boundaries under the British North America Act. Thus the province of Newfoundland will lose one of its seven seats. The commission was charged with the very difficult task of dividing the province into six electoral districts in a fair and equitable manner. Under Section 13(a) of the act, they were to be guided in their task by population distribution.
Using this guideline, with the 1971 population of the province at 522,000 this would result in an electoral quota for each district of some 87,000. However, Section 13(b) gave the commission the right to depart from a strict population basis in cases where there are special geographic considerations, such as the size of an area, sparseness of population, and special community or diversity of interest of the inhabitants of any province.
There is a particular problem which must be dealt with in the province of Newfoudland and Labrador. The Labrador land mass is an area of some 110,000 square miles with a scattered population of approximately 30,000 people. The commission in their wisdom had to include this with another district. I, as the member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, was lucky enough to have it added to my district which already stretches along a coastline of some 425 miles. However, if we are to believe in our pledge to the people of Canada to involve its citizens through its members of parliament, then we must be realistic and honour that pledge.
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) has the task of serving a district which is probably larger than mine. It must be clear to everyone, if

the map of Newfoundland were examined, that to enlarge or readjust western or central Newfoundland because of what someone wrote down on paper many years ago is completely unrealistic.
There is only one simple and fair answer. This bill will allow a reassessment of the electoral boundaries to give Labrador a seat in the House of Commons represented by a member of their choice to serve its Canadian citizens who have been isolated for too long.
I think it is worth mentioning that under our present system the direction of effort in our society is to induce Canadians to go to urban centres. If this trend continues, and with the concept of representation by population, the concentration of representation will be in the urban centres. Further, the political approach toward development will negate the opportunity for Canadians in rural Canada.
There is the danger of ignoring the great and vast resources of places like Labrador and northern Newfoundland, which have been neglected for too long. These isolated communities are always the lowest on the priority scale when it comes to the need for better communications systems and other public services.
There is already a trend toward people going back to rural Canada because of the rat race one has to contend with in the urban jungles in Canada. Surely this emphasizes the need for a new concept of representation taking into consideration the geography of our country.
I read somewhere a statement by an expert that in the 1890's or 1990's everyone in Canada will be concentrated in five or six centres across the country, one of them being Toronto. After listening to the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn), I think all the people in Canada will be moving to Mississauga.
I feel reasonably certain that the member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, who now serves that section of the province with great ability, will agree that a readjustment must come about and that a reduction in the number of seats will make it much more difficult to give Newfoundlanders, not only in Labrador but also in northern Newfoundland, the representation to which they are entitled.
I hope also that he will not mind my concentrating on this part of the province since we represent districts side by side, and, further, since under the new boundaries Labrador would be included in my district of Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe and will be known, I believe, as Humber-West Coast-Labrador.
I am sure my hon. friends from Newfoundland will bring up other points from the knowledge they possess of their districts and will point out the need to increase representation because of the vast outport character of the province stretched out along the coast, where many hundreds of fishing communities exist, all of which require devoted representation. This cannot be accomplished by reducing the representation.
Under the bill now before us, Mr. Speaker, parliament will have 18 months to find an alternative to the proposals of the ten electoral boundaries commissions. There cer-
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension tainly is need for reform. Postponing redistribution provides time to avoid the unpleasant prospect of half the provinces of Canada losing seats in the House of Commons.
I hope this bill will pass after all hon. members have had an opportunity to make a plea for the interests of their own particular districts and that we will immediately deal with the consideration of the changes necessary to bring Canadians the representation they deserve in a fair, equitable and humane manner for the betterment of our nation.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with some care to the arguments which have been made in favour of this bill. In particular, I listened with care to the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) who opposed the bill. I, too, oppose the bill, but I wish the hon. member for Peel South had used some of the other arguments which were available to him rather than those he did; I do not think the ones he used did credit to members who oppose the bill. I believe there are good and legitimate grounds for opposing the bill, grounds which are not related to narrow or special interests.
The speeches made so far in this debate show that members who represent large rural areas are, generally speaking, in favour of the bill. I have yet to hear any argument which deals directly with clauses 2 and 3, which hoist the effect of the recommendations of the redistribution commissions. The argument is this; we need a hoist for 18 months in order to effect the kind of changes necessary in constitutional fairness.
Why cannot the process continue? Why should it be necessary to hoist the effect of redistribution? I see no reason a committee of the House cannot be formed to deal with the subject and allow the commission to continue its work. I have no difficulty in accepting the argument which calls attention to the technical problem which arises because the Chief Electoral Officer would be unable to effect the necessary changes if an election were called in the near future. That is a legitimate contention. But why is there any need to hoist the effect of the law? The only reason appears to be that some provinces are going to lose seats. I submit that it is not beyond the ingenuity of man to solve this problem quickly. A number of solutions are immediately available on an interim basis. The effect of what we are doing in this bill will be to compound an injustice to two provinces-British Columbia and Ontario. I have yet to hear an argument which deals with this issue.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) who also opposed this bill. He told the House that he had travelled through Saskatchewan and found it had been denuded of population. Well, Mr. Speaker, I know where the population has gone. It has gone to British Columbia. Most of these people live in my riding. I hope those members from Saskatchewan will keep in mind, when they vote on this bill, that their expatriates would like to enjoy fair representation, as they used to in Saskatchewan when the population there was greater.
Many arguments have been put forward about the question of rural and urban ridings. I suspect a red herring here. First, there is a substantial provision in favour of

July 6, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension rural constituencies contained in the law presently in effect. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) indicated he was unhappy about the size of his riding. This is a matter which can be looked after under the law as it stands. There is no need to hoist the law in order to bring about changes in that respect.
The fact is that areas whose populations are falling, or increasing at a slower rate than populations elsewhere, enjoy the benefit of a large number of safeguards. First, there- is the provision for Senate representation. No province can lose any of the Senate seats allotted to it and its representation in the Commons must not fall below that number.
Then there is the section of the British North America Act, Section 51, which imposes a 15 per cent limit on any change. Whenever redistribution takes place, representation in a province cannot drop more than 15 per cent. There is also the provision that no province can be represented by fewer members than one of smaller size. For example, New Brunswick has 10 seats because it has 10 Senators. Newfoundland has seven. The difference in population is very narrow. It is entirely feasible that were Newfoundland to gain 100,000 population the province would increase its representation by three members, because it would have to be brought up to the level of New Brunswick. My argument here is intended to demonstrate that a lot of constitutional protection is already given to rural ridings, so I do not weep too many tears when I hear some hon. members cry because they are losing one seat.
Let me draw attention to the situation in British Columbia. The last census which was effective in terms of our representation took place in 1961. Our population at that time numbered about 1,600,000. If this bill goes through we shall have no chance to gain any benefit from redistribution until some new formula has been worked out, perhaps not until the mid-seventies or later. By 1971 our population had grown to 2,200,000. In the course of ten years we gained more than the entire population of Newfoundland. So the effect of this bill, if it is passed, would be to compound an injustice to my province.
The argument presented by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) and others is this: we shall develop a workable formula within a period of time. I do not have much confidence that the House will develop such a formula. I have been listening to the regional jealousies expressed around the chamber and I am not at all sure we shall be able to arrive at a workable formula. The result of this hoist may well be that in July of 1975 we shall be right back where we are today, and the injustice perpetrated against Ontario and British Columbia will continue. This is just not fair.
Consider some of the other anomalies which arise. The hon. member for Peel South emphasized his urban problems somewhat excessively, I thought. Frankly, I feel sympathy with the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and with hon. members from other very large ridings, and I believe special provision should be made to assist them. My argument is directed to the necessity for this proposed hoist. Why should it be vital? The hon. member for Yukon needs help, of course, and perhaps more representation. We cannot be narrow about this question and approach it on the basis of provincial considerations alone. There has

to be some kind of compromise. What I am suggesting is that we have always had compromise, and the people who are working toward the hoist of this bill are the people who want a larger compromise. I think we should turn our attention once in a while to the needs of the urban riding, because the problems arising in this country in future will be in the urban areas.
There is not enough time spent in this House dealing with the question of urban transportation, urban pollution and urban crime, which is becoming a national problem. It seems to me that when we are dealing with the question of representation we might consider how much time we are allocating to urban problems versus rural problems. I suggest to you that question in respect of wheat, oil and national transportation have used up a lot of the House's time at the expense of city problems.

But we get oil. Somebody once said that the problems of this country have developed in this way. First of all, we have the federal government with all the money; then we have the provincial governments with all the jurisdiction; and finally, we have the city governments with all the problems. The effect of this bill is to increase the cities' problems by reducing representation, and I suggest that is unfair.
We have spent $1,350,000 of taxpayers' money on this commission so far. A lot of competent and skilled people have spent a lot of time on this task, and their work is almost complete. I understand the report will be presented in the fall. I urge this House to allow this commission to complete its work. The solution to this problem is not an easy one, and the efforts of some hon. members in the House have not helped. I do not think this measure will bring about a quicker solution.
I agree completely with that clause of the bill which suggests that we should not allow the effects of redistribution to complicate the immediate problems. I am sure the opposition would like the opportunity to bring on an election, just as the government would when the time is right and appropriate; but the delaying effect of the bill would simply compound the injustice to certain provinces, and I do not think this should be allowed to happen.
What are the solutions? We could suggest an immediate freeze so that no province would lose members without restricting representation in those fast-growing areas of Canada, and there must be a reasonable compromise in respect of rural areas. Perhaps a better solution is a floor that could be developed on the basis of square miles versus population; and perhaps in some way we could devise and implement an acceptable formula throughout the country to stop this anomaly in respect of representation in Prince Edward Island.
The hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) represents a riding with a population of about 172,000 as compared to the riding of the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald), who represents just over 20,000 people. I might say that I have been in Cardigan and I know that you can ride around it on a bicycle in a day. It is not a giant community.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this bill which will suspend the present redistribution scheme until such time as we can give some real thought to better methods of achieving equity in respect of this very serious matter. I happen to represent a riding which, as a result of the first proposal of the redistribution commission in Ontario, was completely wiped out. In the second proposal it was brought back almost intact. I must support the committee in its work, not just because it brought the riding back intact, but because of the fact that the problems it faced were tremendous.
I perceive two basic problems. The first relates to the whole idea of community of interest. It is very difficult for a commission in a province the size of Ontario to obtain this community of interest. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) has forgotten that there is some cleavage between southern and northern Ontario. I think I am the third or the fourth member of the government to speak in favour of the bill. When you have a province this size it is very difficult for any group of people to come into a community and understand the situation.
Even though my riding was wiped out and brought back almost intact by the second proposal, the commission left out a very small area, approximately 100 acres, which is the heart of the community. This is the part where the old families and even the grandparents still live. They were cut right out of the riding, yet this was the part of the community which was known as the city of Fort William.
This is the kind of community of interest I suggest a commission from outside is not able to perceive. A lot of redrafting of boundaries has been done, but the effect has been to cut across some of these very important lines of community of interest.
The other basic problem this commission had was in respect of the great variation in the size of ridings in Ontario. One hon. member suggested earlier there was a 50 per cent variation up and a 50 per cent variation down. Actually it is a 25 per cent variation up and a 25 per cent variation down. This is not really a significant variation, but I would ask those of you who have seen the maps to look at the new riding of Albany-Nipigon. It is an unbelievable monstrosity. At the east end it borders on the Quebec border, and on the west it runs just 150 miles from
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension Winnipeg. It goes to the Manitoba border at the James Bay-Hudson Bay point and from there to Lake Superior. How does a member deal with the people on the shores of Lake Superior, and be in contact with the people in Winisk at the other end?
One of the points raised for consideration by the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) was the idea of accessibility. It seems to me one of the principles that apply is that if you have representation you have access to that person representing you. But how is a member who is in Cochrane going to be accessible to people in Winisk, 500, 600 or 700 miles away? This is the kind of problem that this commission had in northern Ontario resulting from the difference in population size between the two censuses. There was a growth rate increase of 5 per cent between the two censuses, while at the same time we lost two seats in northern Ontario, though admittedly one of these seats was reinstated as a result of the second proposal.
These are two of the very difficult problems that faced the commission, and the members frankly admitted they saw no way of really doing an appropriate job unless the variation of 25 per cent was increased. I think a 33 per cent variation would probably have left the boundaries of the ridings in northern Ontario intact. However, the commission had no choice but to work within its limits.
I think there are other implications we have not considered, and I should like to deal with them for a few moments. Canada is a country of great conflict and contrast. We have areas of strong growth, particularly in that triangle from Montreal to Ottawa to Toronto, including the golden horseshoe. Vancouver is another area with a heavy growth concentration. The golden horseshoe is an area of great economic wealth, and I suggest that political power goes hand in hand with economic power.
There is one interesting thing about the golden horseshoe that I am surprised the hon. member for Peel South did not mention. I refer to the fact that in Toronto there is a growing concern about overgrowth, about becoming too big.
I hear hon. members from the golden horseshoe area, especially metropolitan Toronto, talk about the Pickering airport and say that we do not need it. They talk about a greenbelt in the province of Ontario to prevent this kind of growth. Is this the kind of situation in which we should concentrate more and more political power when we want to accommodate a situation of new growth? In the out-lands of this country-and I represent such an area-there are decreasing populations in percentage terms in respect to other areas, and there are lower growth rates. If this bill should pass we would have a considerably declining political power. The wealth of this country, the oil which has been referred to, the power and the energy, must come from these outland areas. We hear people beginning to say we should be doing some of the processing in these areas, that we should be doing some of the secondary as well as primary processing.
We need growth in our area. If it is said that Toronto has grown too much, then why is it not said that we should use whatever resources we have for the purpose of moving the

July 6, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension growth out? We have such plans as DREE and ARDA. Political power is needed in these areas to bring this about. I believe we should at least retain the political power we have at the present time.
I would be very concerned if I were the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) and had a riding containing close to 200,000 people. I do not think there is any justification for having a riding of that size, and I understand his problem. However, I think when we look at ridings like the Northwest Territories, Kenora, Nipigon, Cochrane, or these unbelievable ridings which are being created and which will be far worse than those we have had in the past, even a population of 50,000 may be too large. I think this bill will give us time in which to consider very carefully the needs of the country and allow us to develop some notions in respect of redistributing growth, leaving some political power in those areas where the growth should be.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to enter this debate. At the outset I wish to say I support the bill which is before us. I want particularly to congratulate those hon. members who have brought pressure to bear on the government in urging it to take steps to postpone the implementation of the newly drawn boundaries and to re-examine the electoral mechanism with the ultimate aim of providing for a more equitable system of representation.
I should like also to state that I wish particularly to congratulate the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who was instrumental in bringing this issue before the House. I know also that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) had some very apparent interest in this matter and I congratulate him for the influence he may have had on the government in this particular case. I suspect he may not have been too happy about facing the right hon. gentleman in the next election.
This 29th Parliament is somewhat different from the usual Parliaments we have experienced in the past. The make-up of the House, I believe, is unique. The situation is rather fluid. In the normal course of events members of parliament who were elected in 1972 would serve their constituency for a period of four years. I believe the electorate also anticipate that they would have as their representatives for the next four years those whom they elected in 1972. In the normal course of events an election would not be held until 1976 or perhaps 1977, and during

that period of time the readjustment process could take place in an orderly fashion.
Given that fact, I find it difficult to understand the objections of some hon. members to having the new boundaries postponed until the end of 1974. I really cannot understand the hue and cry, because in the normal course of events we would be functioning with the existing boundaries until 1976 or until 1977.
I believe it is fair to let the electorate know where it stands in so far as who will be its representatives at least until the year 1974. I also believe it is fair to let the elected representatives know where they stand. I think it is true- many members have alluded to this fact-that an election in this minority parliament could occur at any time and could certainly create a great deal of confusion, depending upon the stage of the implementation of the boundaries. Normally anyone who has aspired to office would know exactly where the boundaries of his constituency were. The sitting member of parliament would under normal circumstances know whether ne was functioning on the basis of existing boundaries or whether in the next election he would be looking at a modified constituency or even a new constituency. If we were to have an election this fall, in the spring or perhaps next summer, as has been suggested by some members, we would function on the basis of the existing boundaries.
I find no objection to the extension of the existence of the boundaries we have now until the end of 1974. This bill simply sets out to define the boundaries should an election be called any time prior to 1974. I certainly find nothing wrong with that, and in view of the present circumstances I think the measure will provide some order and stability. It will define boundaries for sitting members, for those aspiring to office and for the electorate at large, and I believe this is important. I also believe the proposal is reasonable and responsible.
The second objective of the bill is to examine, and hopefully prescribe, a new mechanism for the establishment of new electoral boundaries, and to consider, among other things, the desirability of increasing the membership of the House of Commons. I certainly agree with that proposal. Under the current redistribution process we know that the provinces of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Quebec, Manitoba and Saskatchewan stand to lose seats, so I believe this point must be considered very seriously, particularly in light of the fact that this may have a serious and a detrimental effect on the electoral power and the electoral process of the rural areas of Canada.
It is worthwhile noting that even those provinces which do not stand to lose seats under the redistribution process now before the House will lose rural representation very heavily. These rural ridings are swelling to unmanageable proportions, and as a rural representative I simply cannot accept this proposition. The province of Alberta, while maintaining its level of 19 seats, stands to lose three rural seats, and I believe that is wrong. I will have more to say about this in my remarks later, but I believe that in the process of redistribution the commission failed to take into consideration the 25 per cent tolerance factor as well as some of the rural realities which should be considered.
Hon. members have expressed concern about the lack of representation for large numbers of voters in urban con-
July 6, 1973

stituencies. Undoubtedly they have a valid point. However, I think that it can be countered with the argument that the enormous rural areas which will emerge as a result of the redistribution process will deny many rural people the right to effective representation.
The size of some of these rural ridings is enormous. They cut across natural boundaries and they cut across special community of interests. Among other things, many people in the rural areas are confused by the whole electoral process. The electoral boundaries within which we are now operating have served us for two elections. Many people have become used to the fact that they belong to one constituency, but now they are being tossed back into another constituency in which they voted five or ten years ago. Certainly there is no absolute way in which the rural people will get the kind of representation to which I believe they are entitled, at a time when government has a great deal more influence, and in many cases interferes to a much greater extent, in the everyday course of their lives, if we allow our rural boundaries to expand ad infinitum.
I believe it is wrong and totally undesirable that the provinces which I mentioned should lose seats. I believe it is wrong and undesirable that we should emasculate our rural areas through simple mathematical formulae. While the problem may not be totally overcome, I believe we must take steps to alleviate this difficulty at least partially, and if we cannot overcome it completely the process should be slowed down.
So I welcome the review process which will come about as a result of the passage of this bill. I believe we must seriously consider the advisability of increasing the number of seats in the House, and to this end I hope that this measure will make some headway.
I say this for a number of reasons. First, as I said before, the federal government is involved more deeply today in the affairs of individual Canadians across Canada, so naturally the workload of individual members is much heavier and the demands are greater. I think the role of a member of parliament can be divided into three basic parts: his role as legislator, his role as an ombudsman to his people, and his role as a communicating link. All of these roles are very important.
We must also recognize the fact that parliament now sits nine to ten months of the year, and the expansion of rural ridings in particular makes accessibility to the people individual members represent very difficult. I believe that the sheer size of some of the rural ridings that have emerged as a result of the redistribution process will make it physically impossible for many rural members of parliament to serve their areas effectively.
Some hon. members have mentioned the fact that perhaps we should be provided with additional secretarial staff, executive assistants, and so forth. While this may be a partial solution, I do not believe it would provide a satisfactory answer. I think constituents who have a problem with the policies of the federal government want to deal with their elected representative, not with a secretary or an executive assistant. This may work to a degree in
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension some urban areas, but I think in practice it would be ineffective in rural areas.
Many hon. members have mentioned the uniqueness and the diversity of interests in rural areas. I must reiterate this point, particularly in view of some of the speeches that were made by urban members. The rural riding consists of several communities. We have some metropolitan areas within the boundaries of rural constituencies. We have labourers and farmers, and we have some industry. In many areas there is a national park which requires extra special attention. We have Indian reserves and innumerable municipalities, towns, and chambers of commerce. Agriculture is the basic industry in most of the rural ridings, and as it happens most of the policies which affect agriculture emerge from the federal government. So it is the federal government upon which the people engaged in agriculture depend rather than the provincial or local governments. I think urban ridings have better access to government offices. Most cities have representatives of the various departments located there, which is not the case in rural areas.
I hope that in the formula devised as a result of the reviewing process that is anticipated in this bill many of these realities and circumstances will be taken into consideration. I believe we must acknowledge the fact that Canada is a vast country which extends from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean and that the problems of the west are not those of the east. The viewpoints of members of parliament from British Columbia or the prairie provinces differ from those of Ontario or Quebec. Of course, within these provinces also there is a great divergence of opinion. However, I want to point out that, whatever the formula devised, I hope those charged with responsibility for administering the formula will be obligated to follow the rules which are established. If not, there should be some alternative course of action. In my opinion, this has not necessarily been the case in respect of the present act under which we have been operating, particularly in the last redistribution process.
I could refer here to the province of Alberta where the Electoral Boundaries Commission completely disregarded the 25 per cent tolerance factor and the uniqueness of rural areas. I want to say, with all due deference to the learned members who have served on the Electoral Boundaries Commission for Alberta, that they did a lousy job. May I call it four o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

July 6, 1973
Criminal Code (Abortion)
[ English]

subsubtopic: REPEAL OF ABORTION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
that Bill C-34, to amend the Criminal Code (abortion), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
She said: Mr. Speaker, this bill standing in my name has been on the order paper for a number of sessions now. This year it is accompanied by one sponsored by my colleague, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt). Both are designed to do what the government's bill of 1969 failed to do-that is, to bring the matter of abortion into the twentieth century.
The 1969 legislation widened the grounds for legal abortion to some extent but left the glaring injustice of the situation unchanged. Domestic and other pressures have kept the government policing the bedrooms of the nation, despite the fact that over 60 per cent of the citizens have declared their belief that the decision on abortion should be made solely by the woman concerned and her doctor.
The New Democratic Party is well aware of the deep differences of opinion regarding abortion, and this is precisely the reason the bill proposes to take abortion out of the Criminal Code and make it the medical and moral issue it actually is. Abortion has no place in the Criminal Code of this nation.
The passage of this bill would permit those who believe in the necessity for abortion to seek it legally as other medical procedures are sought. Those whose conscience is opposed to abortion would continue, as now, to have nothing to do with it, but as legislators we would have put an end to the present unfair and cruel legal situation which permits a minority to force its will on the majority of the citizens.
[ Translation]
Early in April 1973 Le Devoir published two editorials signed by the editor, Mr. Claude Ryan. Mr. Ryan wondered quite seriously whether the sections of the act dealing with abortion had not been made obsolete by subsequent events. He referred to two recent events which and I quote:
... lead one to believe that in this delicate issue, the law has perhaps lagged behind real life.
The first signal was given in La Presse on March 19 when Claudette Tougas, a reporter described how, during the previous weekend, she had witnessed legal abortions performed in New York State on some thirty Quebec women.
Mr. Ryan would have liked to read:
"an article more concerned with understanding the painful reality hidden behind the decision to have an abortion".
But he made the following comment:
The brutal fact was nonetheless made painfully clear. Every week, Canadian citizens cross the United States border to seek a

'service' that they could not obtain at home under the same conditions.
The other signal came from a doctor made famous by the legal difficulties he has encountered for having performed abortions under conditions not in accordance with the laws of Canada. Dr. H. Morgentaler boasted that he had performed some 5,000 abortions over the past few years, and invited Mr. Claude Castonguay to approve his abortion clinic.
Reflecting on those two signals, Mr. Claude Ryan expressed his opinion in these terms:
Regardless of what one may think of abortion from the moral point of view, these facts force one to wonder whether present laws correspond to the social reality of 1973. To say the least, one must recognize that it is very doubtful. One can rightly question whether the present legislation is efficient, as well as whether it always reflects the real convictions of the citizens.
And I continue the quotation:
As far as efficiency goes, the new law passed in 1969 has given undeniable results. In addition to the fact that those results have been very patchy from one province to the other, every day brings proof that they fall far short of reality.
| English]
Now let us turn to Canada's other great central province, the province of Ontario. Under the editorship of Doris Anderson the magazine "Chatelaine" has shown itself capable and courageous when it comes to leading modern crusades. Ten years before the present abortion legislation was passed it was pressing for legalized abortion, and it is still at it.
In a signed editorial in the June, 1973 issue Doris Anderson refers to past events and to the 1969 legislation in these words:
But the law doesn't work. Some doctors won't have anything to do with helping a patient get an abortion. No Roman Catholic hospitals will perform abortions on the liberalized grounds, so in a town with only a Catholic hospital women find it almost impossible to get an abortion. Many women still have to go to the back street butchers or, if they can afford it, go out of the country to get abortions.
She continues, and I agree with her completely:
Let's make it clear right here that no one is suggesting that birth control is not preferable to abortion.
And may I add that in my opinion abortion is not the first line of defence against an unwanted pregnancy. It is not a desirable method of birth control where contraceptives are available.
Nor are we suggesting that anyone whose religious beliefs do not allow birth control or abortion is being pressured to go against her convictions in having or performing an abortion. But contraceptives sometimes fail. Ignorance and irresponsibility can't be legislated out of the human race. And birth control information in Canada has only been legally available since 1969 and is only patchily available today.
"Patchily available" is right. A search a year ago by the Department of National Health and Welfare found in all of Canada 26 family planning clinics operated by local health clinics, 22 hospital clinics, and 16 run by voluntary agencies. There are also services available in some general health units.
In May, 1972, the then president of the Family Planning Association of Canada, Dr. R. M. Roulston of Winnipeg, stated in Ottawa that provincial and municipal governments "are not establishing sufficient or adequate facilities for family planning." He found Canada particularly
July 6, 1973

deficient in making those services available to native people and to young people. He stated that statistics show that about 20 per cent of all induced abortions are in girls of 18 or under. No wonder that this year's president, Dr. Lise Fortier of Montreal, urged in May in Vancouver that "contraceptive pills should be made available through whoever meets the health needs of the community-nurse, pharmacist, storekeeper."
In my view those people who are today using all their energies and emotions in fighting to keep abortion in the Criminal Code would do well to look at the consequences. They are certainly not preventing abortion by so doing, but they are forcing women who can afford it to seek abortions in other countries or other parts of Canada. They are forcing low income women or those who live in remote areas to run the risk of employing the incompetent and illegal practitioner. They are forcing young people to remain in a state of ignorance and confusion about sex and pregnancy. They are forcing women to give birth to unwanted and unneeded children. They are forcing the majority of the Canadian people to keep a law which, they believe, is unjust and completely unable to meet the needs of today.
Other countries are waging more vigorous campaigns of birth control and sex education than we are in an effort to create that assumption of personal responsibility without which no law involving people can work effectively and well. A recent United Nations report states clearly that in none of the countries where abortion has been liberalized by legislation does it appear that abortion is "advocated as a desirable method of fertility limitation."
That is probably part of the reason why last, February within one week 551 doctors in France, including four Nobel Prize winners, signed a declaration calling for the liberalization of the ancient abortion laws of that country. Each of these medical men confessed either to having performed an abortion in the past or to having assisted women who sought abortion. In taking such action they risked a ten year jail term and a fine of up to $15,000. But like our own Dr. Morgentaler they have found themselves unable to wash their hands of the matter and piously leave women to suffer the tortures and dangers of a pregnancy which they did not want, for which they were only parly responsible, and which, in far too many cases, they did not know how to prevent.
This is the reality and the hypocrisy of the whole matter of keeping abortion in the Criminal Code. This is where the injustice lies. I have tried to keep my remarks in low key, without touching on those horrors so often depicted graphically and in words when this matter is discussed. I want this to be a cerebral discussion. I want the facts to decide what we ought to do.
So, Mr. Speaker, I come once again to the terms of my bill. Briefly, it asks that we do with abortion what we have already done with birth control. Incidentally, the action eventually taken had been resisted fiercely since about 1870, when, I think, birth control was first included in the Criminal Code. We ask that like birth control, the abortion provisions be deleted from the Criminal Code and left as a matter to be decided between doctor and
Criminal Code (Abortion)
patient. Only in this way can we get rid of a bad law which is forcing people to resent its dishonesty and to circumvent it in any way they can.
If the government is unwilling to finish the job it started in 1969, I urge it at least to send the subject matter of this bill to a committee, where the long-evaded public debate the government has promised even since 1972 may find a proper forum. We hope that from such a committee there will come a report that will bring Canada abreast of the very challenging times in which we live.

subsubtopic: REPEAL OF ABORTION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I must congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) for always returning to the highly controversial question of abortion. I know that through Bill C-34, she wants all that to be deleted from the Criminal Code in order to lighten the burden of the innocent victims of those mishaps of youth and of those accidents due to the emotional disturbances of the September years.
At any rate, Mr. Speaker, when a fully affluent society such as ours shows through headlines in the newspapers that abortion on request, abolition of capital punishment for murderers, Olympic Games, shorter working hours and higher salaries seem to have priority in Canada, I wonder whether one should not cast a glance behind, shut his eyes and listen to the roars of the Roman forum, when on the eve of decadence, people used to shout: "Bread and games!" I believe there are much more important things in Canada than those emotional problems and that although they deserve looking into, they should be the last on the list.
The hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway mentioned as an authority the man who, in Quebec is sometimes a pope, sometimes a prophet, sometimes a moralist, and sometimes a president, namely Mr. Claude Ryan. Had he lived in ancient Chaldea, I think he too could have written something on abortion, but he would not have changed anything that happened since man has been dealing with abortion, namely since 4,600 years B.C.
I believe abortion is something against nature and that one must resort to it only in an exceptional case, as provided for in the present legislation in Canada. And it is only because it goes against nature that abortion has been a controversial subject since 4,600 years B.C.
Going back to the most ancien known writings on abortion, dating from 2,000 B.C. we find that Chaldeans decreed the death penalty against a man who had attacked a free man's daughter, as opposed to a slave's child, and had raped her. If this girl died the aggressor's daughter was killed. Of course, the penalties were much less severe if the girl was a slave.
We can also talk about what was going on in the XIth century. We can also talk about the Old Testament. We can as well retrace certain Egyptian texts dealing with the prohibition against abortion. But in Gaul the woman was glorified. She is described as being beautiful, with a lovely figure, tall, of indomitable courage, prolific, an excellent nurse, skilful in farming and in conception, sowing children and wheat. She was the symbol in the Gaul life of the strength forever creating while man was often only a destroying force.

Criminal Code (Abortion)
The Gauls had the right of life and death over their wives and children. One can look back to the days when Hippocrates, the father of medicine, said in his oath, and I quote:
I will give no deadly drug to any, though it be asked of me, nor will I counsel such, and especially I will not aid a woman to procure abortion.
Hippocrates went further, even giving midwives the details of a preparation liable to provoke delivery. It must be noticed that in the days of Hippocrates abortion went unpunished if provoked when the foetus was not alive.
One can also refer to the days of Aristotle, or even Plato, who asked that abortion be mandatory for women over 40. And in ancient Rome abortions were often practised but in a clandestine way.
In the days of the Roman Republic and under the Empire it seems there was a trend towards this type of abortion which was becoming increasingly frequent. It must be noted that at that time if a parents agreed to the abortion it went unpunished and I said earlier the foetus was part of the mother and there was no punishment as long as the baby was still in the embryonary state.
But what is surprising is that if one looks back again to those ancient times Ovid reports that in Rome women between the ages of 25 and 30 were considered old. And today in our society of abundance I wonder if we will not go back somewhat in time to prove in a vivid way that there is nothing new but new men.
And they were saying that women were old at 30 and they had to be aborted so they would preserve the beauty of their bodies and the flexibility of their muscles and therefore they should not longer conceive. They wanted to keep a youthful and attractive chest, a smooth belly and the rosy hue of their skin.
However, there was a violent reaction from the state and Cicero can be quoted as saying:
It destroys the hope of a father, the mainstay of his name and his race, the heir of his family and a citizen meant for the Republic.
Mr. Speaker, the abortion issue has surely been widely discussed and it will continue to be. But as I said at the beginning, when dealing with an anti-natural problem, we constantly run the risk of being waylaid which would prevent us from implementing further the legislation approved by the federal government.
I think that this legislation was normal, since the Criminal Code did not include any clause to protect the medical profession whose members had, at times, to perform such operations to save the endangered life of a mother.
I feel that law is wise because a study of the history of abortion throughout the countries of the world reveals that, at some time or other in their history, they had to rescind their laws which often were too lax, specially with regard to abortion. I am thinking of Russia and Switzerland, but not of France which still has very ancient and conservative methods in this regard. But even today, pressures are being exerted in France which are making the headlines. But I am convinced that the French government

will not change the law of 1920 nor the amendment adopted, I believe, in 1942.
As for England, it is now considering rescinding the law because it is so law that I believe there has been abuse. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, when one looks at the statistics of various countries, and especially Japan, one realizes that the number of suicides has increased appallingly among women who had abortions.
As a doctor, I can assure the House of this: an abortion does provoke a psychological shock in the young girl who has had "an accident of nature".
I do not want to enter into the details of the life of these men who made history. I do not want to talk about the theories of Thomas Aquinas, of his master Albert Magnus I do not want to speak about the quarrels of Alphonso de Liguori neither of Aristotle who claimed that male people or men-for those who do not know that male men- received a soul 40 days after conception whereas the women got one 80 days after, and I wonder why.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, I think that the matter of the foetus is quite debatable but one thing is certain, I cannot understand the attitude of those who are in favour of the abolition of the death penalty for murderers but who are in favour of abortion on a very large scale.
There is certainly a contradiction which I cannot understand.
If today we can admire Canada and especially the province of Quebec which has an average rate of birth lower than is the rest of Canada, it is of course by accepting legislation similar to that which has often been accepted by some countries. The age of affluence will no doubt lead us not perhaps to collective suicide but will affect our Canadian dignity us all its forms, especially the birth rate.
The fact that the honourable member wants to amend the criminal code, will not I think solve the problem; some people might perhaps benefit from it, as they will not be prosecuted. In the case of those who had an illegal abortion, especially those who unfortunately had mishaps I think that prosecution in Canada very seldom followed.
I suggest that it is much more important, whether it be provided in the Criminal Code or not, that women who resort to illegal abortion should realize the full implications of their act. We considered thoroughly in committee the contradictory views which were submitted to us, and I recall that at the end, it was difficult to know who was in favour of abortion and who was against it. We finally came to the conclusion that approximately 52 per cent of those who tabled briefs were against abortion, and almost 48 per cent were in favour of a very liberal legislation.
I suggest that the legislator was wise to amend the Criminal Code in this case, so that those people whose job is to save lives would have something to go by in case of legal prosecutions. And it is at the request of the Canadian Bar Association and of the Canadian Medical Association which, in 1966, presented a brief to the government to that end, that this amendment was made. I am very pleased that amending the whole legislation on abortion does not rank with this government as a priority item. At any rate, I think that this legislation is here to stay that is is an excellent one, and that it is designed for all those who can
July 6, 1973

use it, whenever their grounds are justified, when the life of the mother is in danger.
I suggest that this is the best way to continue to apply a legislation which will never be outdated, Mr. Speaker, because for many centuries it has been applied by all other countries which, at a given time of their history, came back to much more rigid punishments and penalties about abortion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: REPEAL OF ABORTION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to go on record as opposing the bill presented by the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) and being debated this afternoon. Before 1954, all abortions in Canada were illegal. The 1953-54 statute specified that abortion was permissible only if the mother's life was in danger. In 1969 the Criminal Code was amended to permit abortion if the mother's mental and physical health was in jeopardy.
In my opinion, the amendment before the House today, Bill C-34, is simply a licence for abortion on demand. In this matter one should not take a partisan stand, but rather each individual must take a personal, ethical and moral stand in line with one's own philosophy of life.
It is irrelevant whether abortion is in the Criminal Code of Canada or is not. The concept of abortion should be rationally and morally comprehensible to each in his own way. If one works from the premise that the fetus is a living human being-and I hold to that position since the scientific evidence of biologists proves without exception that human life begins at conception-then the matter of abortion involves a change in the whole basic concept on which our laws of society are founded, that of equality of all human beings before the law and the dignity of human life. It is useless to have a conference on human rights if we are to deny the primary right to life itself. The measure of a society is in direct proportion to the protection it gives to its weakest members. In this country we should not say there is no room for these innocents because we cannot feed or clothe them.
However, Mr. Speaker, our government has seen fit to place abortion within the legal confines of this country. Before discussing more liberal abortion proposals, it should be mentioned that laws governing abortion must mesh with other social legislation to provide a completely comprehensive approach. Many women find motherhood a happy prospect but resort to abortion because they cannot extricate themselves from difficult living or working conditions. Unless there are sufficient opportunities for them to maintain an acceptable standing of living through fair labour regulations and easier access to day care centres, simply liberalizing the abortion laws will not solve anything.
Recent Canadian studies have uncovered the alarming fact that many women are using abortion as a means of birth control, either because of ignorance or lack of concern. There are a number of steps which in my opinion should be taken in this regard. For example, the Department of National Health and Welfare should withdraw all existing policy statements supporting abortion as a
Criminal Code (Abortion)
method of secondary birth control. It should publish literature emphasizing that abortion is not an acceptable method of secondary birth control.
Another alternative to abortion is, of course, carrying the pregnancy through. There is a consensus among medical authorities that a mother's feelings toward pregnancy in the early months are no indication of her feeling toward the baby once it is born.
In addition, in a classic study in 1961 it was determined that only 6 per cent of the mothers who did not go through with abortion after receiving legal permission for the operation regretted giving birth. In a great majority of cases the woman had not encountered the difficulties she had imagined would arise with the advent of the child, nor had her health been impaired or her marriage rendered unhappy.
It would appear, therefore, that if women carried their so-called unwanted pregnancies to term there would be little detrimental effect to them. Thus, women should be encouraged and assisted in continuing their pregnancies. Further, it has been shown that by supporting women through pregnancy the pressure for abortion significantly decreases. We must therefore be willing to adopt social policies which will reach out to these women and help them in a practical way.
Some of the positive alternatives to abortion, in my opinion, might be set out as follows:
1.	More extensive education about the facts of pre-natal human life.
2.	Counselling services for pregnant women to direct them to health care available to them.
3.	Establishment of agencies to assist distressed pregnant women to carry their babies to term.
4.	Special programs to help unwed mothers: public education to eliminate the social stigma often attached to unwed mothers.
5.	Improved home-maker service and day care centres.
6.	Make low-income housing available suited to family life.
My final recommendation is to change the law so as to protect the unborn human child. The World Health Organization of the United Nations stated in 1948 that member nations were to accord the utmost respect for human life from the moment of conception onward. In 1959 the United Nations adopted the declaration of the rights of the child in supplementation of the universal declaration of human rights. The preamble to this declaration stated, in part, as follows:
Whereas the child, by reason of his physical and mental immaturity needs special safeguards and care, including appropriate legal protection, before as well as after birth ...
I emphasize the word "before" as well as after birth. The declaration then goes on to declare some of the principles adopted:
Principle 4
The child . .. shall be entitled to grow and develop in health. To this end special care and protection shall be provided both to him and to his mother, including adequate pre-natal and post-natal care.
Principle 8

July 6, 1973
Criminal Code (Abortion)
The child shall be in all circumstances the first ro receive protection and relief.
Principle 9
The child shall be protected against all forms of neglect, cruelty and exploitation.
As a member of the United Nations, Canada has already committed itself to uphold the rights of the unborn child. The legislature in the province of Quebec also recognized the humanity of the unborn in its recent amendments to the Civil Code on January 1, 1972 which provide in part as follows:
Article 18. Every human being possesses juridical personality. Whether citizen or alien, he has the full enjoyment of civil rights except as otherwise expressly provided by the law.
The legal recommendation would be that the homicide provisions of the Criminal Code ought to be amended first to guarantee the protection of the law to the unborn and to those whose status as human beings might at some future time be questioned.
In concluding my remarks, may I say I am surprised that the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) has seen fit to introduce this amendment. I am reminded of a speech she made in this chamber on March 30, 1971 at which time she made an appeal to the Minister of the Environment and Fisheries (Mr. Davis) to ban the slaughter of baby seals. During part of that speech she stated this, which is ironic in this context:
The minister could well have added that for years the members of this House have been flooded with letters, postcards, petitions, etc. from people who want to put an end to the senseless and needless cruelty of the seal hunt.
No doubt most members of this House have been flooded with correspondence of the same type from religious leaders, social workers, members of fraternal organizations, mothers, and other concerned citizens, urging us not to support this amendment. Surely these people have as much right to be heard as those who were objecting to the slaughter of baby seals, and I include in their number the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway. It is interesting to note the way in which the hon. member concluded her remarks that evening. She was quoting a well-known journalist on the need to abolish the seal hunt:
We pay prairie farmers not to grow wheat. Why not pay maritim-ers and Newfoundlanders not to kill baby seals?
And the paradox, the irony of it all, Mr. Speaker, lies in the hon. lady's final remark: "Why not, indeed? The good name of Canada is at stake."

Mr. Speaker, once more, we must discuss the abortion issue in this House, and following the motion moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) who would like all provisions concerning abortion removed from the Criminal Code, since we are far from agreeing on this motion, we must put forward our ideas and make our representations.
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be shocking if all provisions concerning abortion were removed from the Criminal Code, because unfortunately, in our society, there is a tendency to kill innocent people and to forgive criminals. If we listened to all the false slogans, we would live in a

topsy-turvy world where innocents would be killed and criminals freed.
This statement may sound drastic, but it is true and accurate, because the concept to the effect that we must respect the life of others must be retained in this House and in our society as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, there are many arguments that could be set forth concerning the human being, the foetus. Some people claim that the foetus is not a human being. I disagree completely on this point and I agree with most medical, religious and social authorities, knowledgeable people who have studied this problem.
Mr. Speaker, in committee several years ago, when the abortion issue was once again before the House, we heard physicians who came to give us explanations and very valid and precise information about the life of the foetus and related human considerations. At that time, we carried on a fight in this House which lasted more than three weeks in an attempt to prevent any liberalization of abortion laws and to prevent the performance of abortions on demand in Canadian hospitals.
The hon. members will recall the numerous arguments that we then put forward. They will also recall the numerous quotations from doctors and medical authorities who agreed with us.
Our point of view, Mr. Speaker, is mostly the total and integral respect for the life which is in the foetus or in the potential human being. Nobody has any right to destroy a foetus, an innocent being, who will become in a few months or a few days a human being.
Mr. Speaker, before going any further, I would like to quote extracts from material that we receive in large numbers on various subjects, and more precisely today I will quote texts on abortion. I would like to quote Pope Paul VI whom, on January 27, 1971, said during a public audience:
Brothers and friends, as you know, there are values which are the touchstones of a civilization; if they are tampered with, man himself is threatened. Therefore, to tamper with human lives, for whatever reason and in any conceivable way, is to disregard one of the essential values of our civilization. Each and every one of us can feel, in his heart of hearts, as an undeniable and sacred principle, a respect for all human life, that which is beginning, which begs to develop or which is declining, but especially that which is weak, unprepared, defenceless, at the mercy of others.
The recent Council strongly insisted on this: all life is sacred. Except in case of legitimate defence, nothing would ever authorize anyone to dispose of anyone else's life, nor of his own. Contrary, if need be, to what is sometimes thought and said around us, let us repeat and repeat again: abortion as well as euthanasia is homicide.
Brethren and friends who are listening to me, this life which is yours, he lives of your parents, of your children of all men, these fragile and so short lives, remains in spite of all painful experiences, our most precious wealth. This is an element of faith for those among us who believe in Christ and to whom the Gospel teaches that our death on earth is the way to eternal life.
From the same document I quote again:
"Human life is sacred." The Hindu-European religious tradition, at the origin of Hinduism, Judaism, Christianism and Islamism, is
July 6, 1973

that all human life, including embryonic life, has a dignity which comes from the relation between man and his Creator.
Before I formed thee in the belly, I knew thee; before thou earnest forth out of the womb, I sanctified thee. (Jeremiah 1,5)
Mr. Speaker, I could quote many other documents that would corroborate what we have so often quoted in this House to demonstrate that the motion before us today is completely unacceptable as far as moral, society and justice are concerned. The foetus wants to live, to be born; society today needs members for tomorrow. We need to build a society, not to call for minor arguments that allow abortions for all sorts of reasons, giving all kinds of excuses.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I regret that the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) has presented such a motion and that is why we cannot accept it because we in parliament must respect human life, the future of our society.

Mr. Speaker, it could appear that all has been said in this House on the abortion issue as that question has been well debated.
We heard a number of erudite speeches on that subject which went from medical to sociological aspects, setting the pros and the cons.
As I do not pretend to be an expert on the subject, I will only give my own views and I am convinced that it is the views of my constituents.
In September 1971, I received from Archbishop Maurice Roy of Quebec City a submission on birth control and abortion which had been reviewed by the Canadian Roman Catholic Episcopate during the conference on human life which took place on April 25, 1971. Doctor Morris who delivered an outstanding address, concluded by these words:
One of the particularities of most advanced societies is their solicitude towards their most deprived members: the poor, the sick, the handicapped, the mentally ill and the forssaken. The more a society grows towards maturity the more it respects dignity and human rights. The duty of the elected leaders of our society is to protect all its members and to provide for their needs so that no individual or group of individuals could be the victim of another person or another group. It is essential that all members of the Canadian society observe the assessment system for the weak, the aged, the disabled and its members without defence in their mother's womb.
That is in brief what our duty as legislators should be. Any argument in favour of abortion has an opposite view. For instance, some people invoke the over-population problem. If we must face this problem, we ought to find other means than killing the youngest members of our society. In fact, are they trying to remedy unemployment by killing the unemployed, to do away with poverty by killing the poor?
Moreover, as a Quebecker, I should be twice as opposed to such a legislation because as things are going in Quebec, we shall soon face the opposite problem if our birth rate keeps on decreasing. In fact, it showed a decrease of about 12.5 per cent last year. What shall we do with all the manpower now responsible for educating our youth, since
Criminal Code (Abortion)
schools are emptying? Where will governments, at all levels, find their revenues if the number of taxpayers levels off or decreases? We now have some unemployed, though in a reasonable proportion, because compared with the rate in other countries, we shall soon face a much more acute problem, that of manpower shortage.
Of course, all these problems could eventually be more or less solved by immigration. But I do not think that this is really a solution which Canadians would want. In any event, I, as a Quebecker, could not be much in favour of immigration for my province as everyone knows the problems which the province is experiencing, particularly in the Montreal region, with the integration of these new citizens into the community.
Furthermore, if only to respect the opinions of my constituents in this matter, I must vote against liberalizing the legislation passed in 1969.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read a letter which I have received from more than 2,000 of my constituents.
Dear Sir,
As my representative the federal government, I strongly request you to oppose Bill C-142, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (abortion).
I am absolutely against abortion! No one has a right to decide whether a human being is to live or not. The promoters of abortion hold that a woman has a right to dispose of her own person. She has no right to sacrifice her child for selfish reasons such as comfort, leisure, financial security, etc.
Indeed, women are entitled to proper guidance, appropriate sexual education, suitable housing, special medical care and adequate protection. She also has a right to bear her child in dignity, no matter what the circumstances are. Our legislators would be much wiser to approach more positively social problems which are a source of worry to our society, instead of evading their duties by condoning the murder of unborn babies. We strongly urge you to make laws favoring the protection and the enhancement of human life.
We hope that you will strongly oppose this bill that would ratify the murdering of an innocent.
Mr. Speaker, I answered that I too was opposed to any extension or liberalization of the present law, that only therapeutic abortions are now allowed and performed in accredited hospitals, only when they are approved by a medical committee, that I considered this law as sufficiently liberal and as not needing to be more liberal.
I shall then abide by what I promised my voters and vote accordingly, that is against this bill which would extend a law that I already deem broad enough.

Mr. Speaker, I wish once again to reiterate my opposition to abortion and to the proposition put forward by my hon. friend from Van-couver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis). It amazes me how an abolitionist such as she can at the same time be in favour of a law that would condone abortion. Just as my hon. friend from Hull (Mr. Isabelle) pointed out a while ago, it seems there is a definite contradiction here. I find it very difficult to understand how someone can be in favour of allowing a known criminal to live yet at the same time advocate that an innocent babe in its mother's womb should be killed. To my way of thinking this is wrong.
It is not only a medical question, it is a moral question. This whole matter has to do with our moral code. Let us not forget that our code was founded on the Judeo-Chris-tian attitude and that morality is one of the things that has allowed us to become a great nation. So far as I am concerned this kind of law will never be passed in this country, and I am glad to know that the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), as long as he is minister, will never allow this kind of law to be passed.
